#5705. Germany’s Hydrogen Pipeline Reached Marl. Its Market Still Needs to Add Up.

Germany’s hydrogen backbone achieved a genuine milestone on August 4, 2026. RWE and its partners announced that renewable hydrogen produced during commissioning at Lingen had reached Marl Chemical Park, roughly 120 kilometres away. Electrolysers, converted natural gas pipelines and industrial receiving infrastructure were working together.

The GET H2 consortium deserves credit for getting the equipment operating. But completing a hydrogen pipeline and establishing an economically competitive market for the hydrogen moving through it are different achievements.

The announcement did not disclose the quantity received at Marl, the price paid by an industrial customer or which existing hydrogen production was displaced. The English release describes hydrogen being available for industrial use, while the German release says it was used. Neither provides the industrial mass balance needed to determine the actual emissions benefit. The network also contained hydrogen from earlier commissioning activities, which makes tracing individual molecules through the pipeline less useful than measuring what changed at the receiving industrial facilities.

Marl is hardly a new hydrogen customer. The chemical park has used hydrogen for decades in integrated production processes. Providing another source may be useful, especially where renewable hydrogen replaces fossil-derived supply, but existing demand does not automatically become commercially viable demand for a considerably more expensive feedstock.

The larger infrastructure ambition makes that distinction important. Germany’s approved hydrogen core network covers 9,040 kilometres and has expected investment costs of €18.9 billion. Much of the network will use converted natural gas pipelines. These are approved plans and anticipated investments, not evidence that the entire network has been built or that future customers have committed to using it.

There are genuine industrial commitments. RWE has a 15-year agreement with TotalEnergies to supply approximately 30,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen annually to the Leuna refinery from 2030. That provides a named customer, volume and contract period. The price is undisclosed, and European fuel regulations help create demand for renewable hydrogen in refining.

That is a much stronger commercial signal than commissioning a pipeline. The question is how many comparable customers exist, what they can afford and whether their businesses will continue using hydrogen over the decades required to recover infrastructure investments.

The wider European outlook has become less optimistic. ENTSOG’s October 2026 draft assessment reduced its 2030 hydrogen demand assumption from 620 TWh to 335 TWh, a 46% reduction from its 2024 assessment. Its 2040 assumption fell 33%, from 1,929 TWh to 1,296 TWh. These are changes to European planning scenarios, not measurements of declining actual hydrogen consumption, but they matter when infrastructure economics depend on demand growth.

My central model of hydrogen supplied through the Lingen system produces an illustrative delivered cost of about €9.06/kg after assumed capital support, compared with a €3/kg conventional hydrogen benchmark. Those are scenario values, not RWE’s actual costs or the undisclosed price paid at Marl. The gap illustrates the challenge facing industrial manufacturers selling chemicals into competitive international markets.

Hydrogen remains an important industrial feedstock. Well-located connections between producers and customers with durable demand may be worthwhile. Germany needs evidence that the customers and products can support the investment, rather than assuming that building enough pipelines will bring the market into existence.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. #5703. Fiery Jet Crash In Florida Kills 9 After Falling 20,000 Feet Per Minute Before Impact

Just seconds after the co-pilot of flight N722BD sent its Mayday final transmission on Sunday afternoon, the private Learjet 60 crashed in a fiery explosion, killing all 9 people on board and raining debris across a South Florida community. As of Monday, authorities are still in the early stages of the investigation, which could take several days to collect wreckage from the fallen aircraft, according to AP News.

According to the National Transportation Safety Board, the business jet took off from Austin, Texas, and was heading towards the Bahamas when it hit the ground in the Palm Beach County neighborhood of Green Acres, near West Palm Beach. Just minutes before the crash, the co-pilot, 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, reported encountering weather causing icing and "moderate turbulence." They asked to ascend to 37,000 feet, which was approved by Air Traffic Control. The plane then began descending quickly, with the co-pilot informing controllers, "We're descending 8,000 — Mayday, Mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute.

One pilot has been identified as of this writing. Filgueiras was a Boca Raton resident who achieved her dream of a pilot's license while still in high school and had 1,300 hours of flying time under her belt. She was the one who made the final emergency calls as the jet went down. Another pilot was aboard the flight as well. It is unclear at this time who was at the controls of the jet when the crash occurred. All nine fatalities were passengers onboard the plane.

During a news conference Monday the NTSB officials said the crash created a debris field  approximately a half mile by four-tenths of a mile, but it may be larger as there is evidence that shows the plane was likely breaking up prior to impact. They've asked members of the community who find debris to not move it and contact NTSB or local authorities to handle it. Officials also said that weather conditions are being considered as a major factor in the events that unfolded Sunday afternoon. More updates are expected to come in the following days.

In the plane's final transmissions, the plane was flying at an altitude of nearly 9,000 feet. The plane then nosedived, falling at 32,000 feet per minute according to CBS News, however, the NTSB said those numbers have not yet been determined or confirmed. Dashcam footage shared with multiple news outlets caught the moment of impact from the back of a moving vehicle on a divided motorway. Another dashcam video obtained by KCEN 6 News, showed the plane falling out of the sky some distance ahead of the vehicle before impact.

Witnesses to the crash told CBS News it sounded like a bomb went off when the jet hit the ground. Stephanie Platts, a resident at a neighboring mobile home community park, told The New York Times she was on her patio with her family when the plane hit, which sounded like a car crash. Her home caught fire from some of the raining debris.

"Everything was engulfed in flames," she said.

Palm Beach County authorities were called to the scene where it was eventually confirmed that all nine passengers on board the business jet had died. Only one individual may have sustained injuries from the crash, who was adjacent to the scene, but officials have yet to confirm that injury.

This crash comes just months after an Amazon Air cargo plane killed five people after landing  late on a Miami runway. Weeks later, a small yellow airplane narrowly missed hitting a postal van while making an emergency landing on an Illinois highway, leaving no crashes or injuries behind.

#5702. Swarm Of Electric Trucks Coming To US (Battery Swapping Included?)

Tesla CEO Elon Musk famously ditched the idea of EV battery swapping back in 2015 after a brief experiment. That pretty much laid the idea to rest here in the US, but other EV stakeholders soldiered on. The latest example is the Australian firm Janus Electric, which is bringing its Class 8 heavy duty electric truck conversions to North America. Janus offers a battery-as-a-service model that includes both charging and swapping…so, is battery swapping finally coming here to the US?.

Battery swapping for two-wheelers and larger EVs is commonplace in some overseas markets, with industry leader Nio being one example. So far, though, swapping stations for e-bikes are the only sign of emerging activity in the US.

Musk’s opinion aside, a modern battery swapping station can change a spent electric car battery for a fresh one in just a few minutes, or less time than it takes to drive through an automated car wash. On the other hand, considering today’s EV fast charging technology, battery swapping is somewhat less relevant to passenger cars and other light duty vehicles. Access to home charging is another factor that can limit the appeal of driving to a battery swapping station for a refresh.

Electric trucks, though, are another kettle of fish. Every minute counts in the fast paced transportation industry. Waiting in line for an EV charging station to free up is a non-starter, and then there’s the charging time. Even the much-heralded Tesla Semi Class 8 truck can take hours to reach a full charge overnight, though the truck is reported to achieve 60-70% charge in as little as 30-45 minutes at fast charging stations.

The time factor explains why battery swapping for trucks is appearing in overseas markets. The seeds of change have also begun to sprout up in the US, where the the diesel-to-electric conversion field is beginning to offer some opportunities. Last summer, for example, the US startup Revoy (formerly SixWheels) announced a swappable battery retrofit for Class 8 diesel trucks. The retrofit consists of a battery unit inserted between the cab and the trailer, which can be swapped out in a matter of minutes. The unit does not replace the engine, but it reportedly cuts diesel emissions by up to 85%, with a 95% fuel savings aided by regenerative braking.

The US Army is also dipping a toe in the conversion field with “idling kits,” which are batteries powerful enough to run on-board equipment for military vehicles in near silence, without the giveaway noise and heat signature involved in idling the vehicle’s engine. No word yet on whether or not swap-outs will be part of the picture, but the technology pieces are in place.

So much for the current state of affairs. Last week a full diesel-to-electric conversion opportunity suddenly appeared when the Canadian lithium-ion battery specialist Electrovaya announced a new $26 million diesel-to-electric supply agreement with the Janus that leverages Electrovaya’s proprietary “Infinity Battery Technology, a durable system compatible with daily swapping cycles for Class 8 trucks.

The $26 million agreement represents just the initial phase of orders for the US and Canadian markets. “Electrovaya has also agreed to invest approximately $1.4 million in Janus for up to 4.2 million shares, together with up to 6.3 million warrants,” Electrovaya noted, indicating a long term partnership allowing plenty of room for scaleup.

“Janus’s approach converts existing diesel prime movers to battery-electric operation and pairs them with swappable battery packs and Janus Charge & Change Stations, allowing fleets to exchange batteries in minutes rather than wait hours to recharge, and to electrify without the capital cost of purchasing new trucks,” Electrovaya explained (see additional coverage on CleanTechnica  here and here).

Janus’s footprint in North American is still tiny, at 118 truck conversion orders and commitments in the US and Canada combined. However, the firm’s business with Electrovaya should help ramp up the activity. Janus has already begun deliveries to Electrovaya, and Electrovaya has announced a major expansion of its North American manufacturing footprint. The showpiece is a production facility in Jamestown, New York covering lithium-ion battery cells, modules, and packs.  Start of operations is schedule for sometime next year.

With US President Donald Trump’s war in Iran continuing to elevate diesel costs, both Janus Electric and Electrovaya smell an end to the partisan war on EVs that rocked the US market after Trump took office in January of 2025. “Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale,” said Janus CEO and Managing Director Ben Hutt in a press statement.

“The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport,” Hutt added.

The CEO of Electrovaya, Dr. Raj Das Gupta, also underscored the potential for rapid scaleup. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations,” Gupta emphasized.

“Our strategic investment, together with the warrants, aligns us closely with Janus’s long-term growth,” Gupta also explained, with warrants referring to up to 6.3 million in contracts for future stock transactions.

If you’re wondering how much traction Electrovaya and Janus will gain in the US electric truck conversion space, that’s a good question considering Trump’s on-again, off-again trade wars with the upstairs neighbors.

The factory in New York State should help push matters along. As if on cue, over the weekend the White House also signaled that Trump is suddenly willing to call off his tariff dogs, potentially leading to a trade deal with Canda that could help accelerate activity in the US electric truck conversion field, among other areas.

On the other hand, the negotiations are described as achieving an early stage “concept” of a deal, which makes it seem more like a weak effort to gin up voter support for the Republican ticket ahead of Election Day on November 3. The concept of a deal could just as easily de-materialize by the morning of November 4.

Deal or no deal, Trump is scheduled to leave office in January of 2029 at the latest — peacefully this time, one hopes — opening up space for a new era of stability and mutual benefit in US-Canada trade relations.

In the meantime, keep an eye on Electrovaya for more activity in the electrification field, with or without help from the US market. In addition to supplying batteries for electric truck conversion, the company anticipates business in the fields of material handling, robotics, defense, and AI data center infrastructure.

#5701. Washington State Resident Dies From Bird Flu Following Exposure to Infected Cattle

— Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since 2024

A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.

The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.

Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.

Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The CDC said the person was infected with H5N1.

County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.

They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.

The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows, and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.

More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.

The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.

Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.

#5700. Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides

Kennedy's HHS relaxes enforcement on 6 popular wellness peptides" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides.

The move, which comes after the same peptides won favor at an FDA advisory committee meeting this summer, is being hailed by some in the industry as offering a more accountable alternative to the gray market many peptide-seekers currently use, while others have charged that it undermines institutional FDA pushback on the drugs, which have become increasingly popular among fitness influencer circles and the MAHA crowd.

Under Kennedy’s “enforcement discretion policy” issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Advisory committee votes are recommendations, not binding decisions, and the peptides still haven’t been added to the drug substances list in an official capacity.

Kennedy cited that meeting in his enforcement decision, alongside data on utilization of peptides, noting that HHS believes there is “significant interest in the use of these peptides in compounding given the lack of availability of approved products.”

The letter clarifies the agency may revisit the interim policy if it leads to new safety signals or product quality issues.

The new policy comes with several other caveats that compounders must satisfy too, including sourcing their bulk drug substance from an FDA-registered facility and ensuring that the ingredients are properly characterized and identified. The original manufacturer of the bulk drug substance must also be registered with the FDA, according to HHS’ document.

In another change from typical compounding practice, compounders will be required to report quality issues and serious adverse events associated with the newly unrestricted peptides that are associated with their use, whether the drug itself is considered related or not, HHS clarified.

Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Traditionally, the compounding practice has focused on the mixing or altering of ingredients of a drug to create a custom medication for a patient.

The practice can also come into play in order to fill drug shortages, which led to the pop-up of a GLP-1 compounding cottage industry for obesity that branded drugmakers Novo and Eli Lilly have continued to grapple with, even after supply shortfalls of their licensed medicines were declared formally ended in the United States.

In a statement Wednesday, Alliance for Pharmacy Compounding (APC) CEO Scott Brunner said he welcomed the decision, noting that it isn’t a question of whether patients are already using these six peptides, but of “where they’re getting them.”

“Right now, far too many patients are obtaining peptides from illicit suppliers with little assurance about what's actually in the vial,” he said. “That's an existing public health threat, and one that isn't going away simply because compounding of the substances is prohibited.”

While noting that the policy now offers a “more accountable alternative” to that murky peptide supply chain, Brunner emphasized the importance of the limits the enforcement action puts in place as well, while also highlighting questions that remain, including when the policy actually takes effect, how API testing and analysis will be validated and how product utilization reporting will work.

“That last point is especially important,” Brunner said. “A credible federal policy with meaningful patient safety safeguards gives states a sound basis for their own oversight and helps discourage a patchwork of state rules and restrictions that could undermine the access HHS is trying to provide.”

Others, including consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, adopted a decidedly more antagonist tone toward the new enforcement policy. In a statement issued this week, the group noted the peptides included in the new list are “popular but unproven and unapproved,” flagging Kennedy’s own personal support of the compounds.

Questions around conflicts of interest among panelists on the PCAC panel were also raised this summer, with the FDA quickly slotting in eight temporary voting members ahead of the confab in a bid to appease some of the criticism.

With the move, Kennedy “has acted recklessly and unilaterally to put Americans in danger,” Robert Steinbrook, M.D., Public Citizen’s health research group director, said in a statement, contending that the HHS secretary ought to “support, not sabotage, needed FDA enforcement actions to protect consumers.”

#5699. The Harley-Davidson Sprint 440 Is Exactly What Harley Needs

It's finally happening: Harley-Davidson is bringing a proper Harley-looking beginner bike to the United States. Not some weird half-baked attempt like the Street line, but a proper Harley-styled cruiser that just happens to be built around a smaller, beginner-friendly engine. The new bike is called the Sprint 440, it's debuting at EICMA, and I couldn't be more excited for it.

I've long said that Harley needs a proper beginner bike, a way into the brand that capitalizes on what Milwaukee does well — vintage, call it "authentic" styling — without the company's usual high prices and general skull-themed accessorizing. The Sprint 440 appears to be just that: A practical single cylinder, a Sportster-esque sloped tank, and a price that lets beginners actually cross-shop Harley with Kawasaki and Triumph. While we don't know the firm U.S. price yet, we know the bike goes for just $8,500 Canadian up north — the equivalent of just over $6,000 here.

The Sprint looks leagues better than the Nightster it displaces as Harley's cheapest bike, with styling that better hides the brake lines, wires, and radiators a modern motorcycle requires. The Sprint could be mistaken for an Iron 883 by those who don't know the ins and outs of both bikes, though it does need some indicators of its foreign coproduction — the bike is a collaboration with India's Hero MotoCorp, according to RideApart, and its chain drive demonstrates that things aren't all Harley here. Still, it's a Milwaukee bike in the ways that really matter: Despite the foreign assistance, Harley says the bike will undergo final production in Pennsylvania.

Harley hasn't yet released all the specs for the U.S. model of the Sprint, but we know the international model has a 26.4-inch seat height (though Harley specifies that's "laden") and a 412-pound weight. Horsepower is low, at just 27, though it makes a full 28 pound-feet of torque. Those numbers aren't incredibly impressive, but if you're a new rider into the looks of a classic Harley you probably won't mind — you'll just appreciate a lighter, cheaper way to get the bike you want. That kind of accessibility is what Harley has been lacking for years, and I truly hope the Sprint 440 helps the brand get some new buyers in.

#5698. As Diesel Costs Surge for Farmers & Rural Businesses, Solar Offers a Lifeline

The cost of diesel fuel rose nearly 33% from 2025 to 2026, with some countries experiencing even higher price spikes. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, solar-powered equipment offers an attractive alternative.

On a dry hillside in Chamwino, central Tanzania, mango farmers used to watch their trees struggle through the long months without rain. Irrigation was technically possible: A diesel pump could lift water from a nearby borehole. But in practice, fuel was too expensive and too unpredictable for smallholders to run the system often enough. When diesel prices rose, farmers irrigated less, production dropped, and most households stayed locked into low-yield farming and razor-thin margins.

In 2021, a solar-powered pump and drip irrigation system replaced the diesel setup as part of a pilot project. Within one season, farmers reported that their mango production and average income from mango sales roughly doubled, as farmers could irrigate beyond the rainy season and manage their orchards more intensively. The technology change was simple—solar instead of diesel. But for farmers, it meant shifting from a fuel prone to wild price swings to an energy source they could rely on and afford.

Chamwino is not an isolated case. Across Africa and other regions, farmers, processors, and rural businesses are among the most exposed to diesel price spikes, like those happening right now. Because diesel powers irrigation pumps, generators, mills, and refrigerators, every price jump shows up as higher operating costs, thinner margins, and greater risk.

Distributed clean energy is emerging as one of the most practical ways to break that dependence.

While access to electricity has expanded significantly over the last 10 years, the reality is that diesel still powers much of rural life in places like sub-Saharan Africa. Only 33% of the rural population can access electricity. Even among those with power connections, frequent outages and poor quality have led farmers, processors, retailers, mines and telecommunications companies to rely on diesel generators for backup or primary power. An Energy for Growth Hub study estimated that 150–190 gigawatts (GW) of distributed diesel generator capacity was operating across Africa in 2024, compared with 268 GW of grid-connected capacity. Removing South Africa from the equation, Sub-Saharan Africa had nearly 1.5 times as much diesel generator capacity as grid-connected capacity. And diesel capacity exceeded grid capacity in at least 26 African countries.

The war on Iran has exposed the vulnerability created by this “shadow power system.” The average global retail diesel price exceeded $1.50 per liter in the second quarter of 2026, 20% higher than the previous three months and 32.9% higher than a year earlier. In Africa, retail diesel prices rose by 25% on average across 42 countries between mid-January and mid-June 2026.

The regional average masks sharp differences between countries. In some, subsidies, tax cuts, and administered fuel prices have cushioned consumers from rising international prices, but at a cost to government budgets, especially in fuel-importing economies with limited fiscal space. Elsewhere, consumers have faced much larger increases at the pump. Diesel prices increased by 86% in Nigeria and more than 50% in Tanzania and Ethiopia from January to June 2026.

The effects extend beyond the cost of running generators. Diesel powers agricultural machinery, irrigation pumps, mills and refrigerators. Diesel-fueled road transport connects farms with suppliers and consumer markets. The impacts of the Iran conflict are already rippling through interconnected energy, fertilizer, trade and logistics networks, raising the costs of agricultural production and food distribution across Africa and elsewhere. Fertilizer prices have increased by 30-45% in several African markets since the conflict began, increasing the risk that farmers will reduce application rates, switch to other crops or miss their planting windows.

The effects are felt most acutely at the local level. For example, members of a women’s groundnut processing cooperative in Nigeria reported that rising fuel and fertilizer costs increased the price of raw groundnuts and groundnut oil by 33%. In Myanmar, which imports more than 90% of its fuel and relies predominantly on road transport, higher diesel prices have increased the cost of moving food and agricultural inputs, and have led to rising rice prices for consumers.

We already have better alternatives. Many locations are struggling with diesel-based irrigation, cooling and backup power, but solar and other distributed renewables can provide more affordable and reliable electricity than diesel-dependent systems.

The shift is already gaining momentum. In Africa, 17 GW of solar capacity will be installed in 2026 — a 45% increase from 2025, equivalent to approximately 100,000 panels installed each day. Much of the recent growth is happening outside large power plants: Roughly three-quarters of Africa’s solar growth between 2023 and 2025 came from distributed systems, as households and businesses sought alternatives to unreliable supply and diesel generation.

The benefits are already visible for some who have made the switch.

Ethiopia’s Berbere district, or woreda, is surrounded by four rivers, yet for years farmers could not use that water for irrigation. Limited access to electricity and the high cost and unreliability of petrol and diesel made pumping water from rivers to fields impractical, keeping production closely tied to rain-fed maize and teff. In 2025, WRI and partners installed two solar-powered water pumps to lift river water to irrigated plots. In the first production season, households involved in the project earned an average $709 from onion cultivation alone, compared with around $207 annually from maize and teff before the solar-powered pumps were installed. Farmers also reported being able to harvest more than once a year, plant surplus crops such as onions and chilies to increase their incomes, and make new investments in livestock and home improvements.

Similarly, when Kenya experienced its longest nationwide power blackout in 2023, one Nairobi hospital maintained critical services thanks to its solar-plus-battery storage system. For rural clinics and county hospitals, similar systems can ensure power even when the grid fails, without tying budgets to volatile fuel prices and expensive back-up diesel generators.

There’s huge potential for distributed clean energy to further break diesel dependence and improve livelihoods in places like rural Africa and elsewhere. Energy Access Explorer, an open online geospatial platform hosted by the WRI Polsky Energy Center, lets planners examine solar potential alongside grid networks, health facilities, schools, and farming communities. Bringing these layers together can help governments and practitioners identify where clean power could cost-effectively serve livelihoods and services that currently depend on diesel.

For example, Energy Access Explorer is already informing electrification planning in Ethiopia. The Ministry of Water and Energy, working with the World Bank, has used the platform to prioritize off-grid electrification through a results-based financing program. Our latest analysis reveals that about 12.6 million people in Ethiopia live in areas with high agricultural activity and high solar potential, but little access to grid-connected electricity. These areas could be assessed for solar-powered irrigation, processing, cooling and other services that could benefit from distributed clean power.

A Uganda analysis applies the same approach to health services. The map below shows 243 health facilities and approximately 4.6 million people living in areas with limited or no connection to electricity. Yet these areas do receive abundant sunlight, making them suitable for solar power. Used alongside data on facility electricity demand, existing supply reliability, and roof or land availability, the maps can help prioritize clean power investments for rural health services.

As diesel prices continue to swing wildly with every conflict and crisis, farmers, processors, and rural businesses pay the price, alongside governments that try to keep costs low through subsidies. It’s time for energy ministers, donors and financiers to look closely at where distributed clean power can viably replace diesel and direct their investments there. The latest Tracking SDG 7 report estimates that $21 billion is needed by 2030 to provide off-grid solar to the 398 million people for whom it is the least-cost electricity option—approximately 6 times the sector’s recent investment level!

Moving from energy crisis to energy security is ultimately about knowing where clean energy truly changes livelihoods. For many of the world’s rural farmers, processors, and small businesses, that starts with swapping diesel for solar.

By Dimitris Mentiss, Lead, Energy Access Explorer

— Mitapivat improved hemoglobin response, but no significant benefit for pain crises

The thalassemia drug mitapivat (Aqvesme) significantly improved hemoglobin response in patients with sickle cell disease but failed to top placebo when it came to reducing pain crises in a phase III trial that aims to support an expanded approval.

In the RISE UP trial, 41% of patients assigned to the oral pyruvate kinase activator had a hemoglobin response, as compared with 3% of placebo recipients (P<0.0001). But that didn't translate into a reduction in the annualized rate of sickle cell pain crises (2.6 for mitapivat vs 3.1 for placebo, P=0.1213), reported researchers led by Biree Andemariam, MD, of the New England Sickle Cell Institute at University of Connecticut Health in Farmington.

Beyond those two primary endpoints, treatment with mitapivat was associated with improved markers of hemolysis, reduced transfusion burden, and additional clinical benefits in the subset of patients with a hemoglobin response, but not with improvements in patient-reported fatigue, the study authors wrote in The Lancet.

These mitapivat data, which are currently under review with the FDA, arrive amid turbulence in the drug market for sickle cell disease. Crizanlizumab (Adakveo), approved in 2019, lost its marketing authorization in Europe after randomized trial data showed the drug failed to top placebo when it came to vaso-occlusive crises, though it's still available in the U.S.

And voxelotor (Oxbryta), which was granted accelerated approval, also in 2019, was pulled from global markets after trial data turned up an imbalance in deaths and acute vaso-occlusive crises for patients on the hemoglobin S polymerization inhibitor.

Mitapivat is currently approved as a disease-modifying treatment for anemia in adults with alpha- or beta-thalassemia, and an approval decision in sickle cell disease is expected by February of next year.

Labeling for mitapivat includes a boxed warning due to the risk of liver injury, which also warranted a risk evaluation and mitigation strategy (REMS) program. The FDA has requested an analysis on whether a REMS would be needed in sickle cell disease, but drugmaker Agios Pharmaceuticals said the data so far have shown no cases of liver injury that follow the pattern or severity seen in the thalassemia trials.

The RISE UP trial was conducted across 69 sites in 15 countries and randomized 207 patients older than 16 years with anemia and recurrent sickle cell pain crises in a 2:1 ratio to twice-daily mitapivat (100 mg) or placebo.

At baseline, participants had a median age of 25 years, 57.5% were female, mean hemoglobin was about 8.5 g/dL, and they averaged 3.4 sickle cell pain crises per year.

The primary endpoint of hemoglobin response was defined as a 1 g/dL or greater increase in average hemoglobin concentration from week 24 to week 52 compared with the baseline.

In a commentary accompanying the study, Jennifer Knight-Madden, MBBS, PhD, and Zachary Ramsay, MBBS, both of the University of the West Indies in Kingston, Jamaica, noted that despite the mixed results on the primary endpoints, "there could be clinical benefit" among the mitapivat responders.

The findings should be interpreted with caution, they noted, but post-hoc analyses suggested the mitapivat-treated participants "who achieved a hemoglobin response experienced lower annualized rates of sickle cell pain crises, fewer related hospitalizations and emergency department visits, longer times to first and second sickle cell pain crises, and lower fatigue scores compared with non-responders."

"The findings provide evidence that a clinically meaningful benefit can exist within a subset of patients," they wrote. "As acknowledged by the authors, this study was not designed to identify patients likely to achieve a hemoglobin response, and differences in hemoglobin response could be due to genetic and epigenetic modifiers, red cell metabolic differences, and co-inherited red cell variants."

As for safety data, mitapivat was associated with lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs), at 33% versus 41% with placebo, and lower rates of serious AEs (20% vs 29%), Andemariam and colleagues reported. One of the serious AEs in a mitapivat-treated patient was considered treatment-related, however.

Overall, AEs leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in 4% of patients in the mitapivat group and in 3% of the placebo group. Despite no signal of liver injury in the study, some hepatic-related AEs did lead to mitapivat discontinuation, including one patient with increases in aspartate aminotransferase (grade 3) and bilirubin (grade 2), another patient with hepatic enzyme increases (grade 4) deemed unrelated to treatment, a patient with hepatic cytolysis (grade 2) and other AEs, and one patient with transaminase increases (grade 2) considered secondary to an infection.

Deaths occurred in 2% of the mitapivat arm and 3% of the placebo arm, with none deemed treatment-related.

NYU Langone brings OpenEvidence’s clinical AI into the EHR systemwide" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

OpenEvidence is expanding its footprint in New York City through a partnership with NYU Langone Health, adding another marquee institution to an existing concentration of partnerships across the city's academic medical centers.

OpenEvidence's AI-powered clinical evidence platform is embedded directly into NYU Langone's Epic electronic health record (EHR) workflows. NYU Langone has more than 12 million outpatient visits annually, 421,000 emergency department visits, seven inpatient locations and over 400 outpatient locations. The integration will span NYU Langone's hospitals, ambulatory network and the Family Health Centers and will also reach physicians who are training at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and the NYU Grossman Long Island School of Medicine.

The system has more than 6,000 physicians and faculty, 2,000+ residents and fellows and 54,000 employees.

“At NYU Langone, we are committed to working with OpenEvidence to make the latest technology available to our clinicians in a safe and practical environment at scale,” said Nader Mherabi, executive vice president and vice dean, chief digital and information officer at NYU Langone Health said in a statement.

OpenEvidence developed an AI-powered medical search engine and a generative AI chatbot exclusively for doctors, which summarizes and simplifies evidence-based medical information. It has grown to become one of the most widely used medical AI and CDS tools in the industry. The company says its "patient-aware clinical intelligence" uses agentic clinical AI to integrate details of the patient record with the evidence from the medical literature.

NYU Langone clinicians will be able to ask complex clinical questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in peer-reviewed medical literature and read against the patient’s own clinical record, all without leaving their Epic workflow, according to OpenEvidence executives.

“NYU Langone cares for New Yorkers at a scale few institutions in the country can match, and it does so while setting the standard of care across specialties,” Daniel Nadler, founder and CEO of OpenEvidence, said in a statement. “New York has always been where American medicine goes to prove itself at scale. Putting OpenEvidence inside the chart at NYU Langone means the world's medical literature is now in the room for every one of the twelve million visits this system supports each year.”

OpenEvidence has already amassed a large following among individual clinicians, with the company saying roughly two-thirds of U.S. physicians use its platform. As of October, there were 1.2 million medical license-verified U.S. clinicians, including physicians and nurses, using OpenEvidence, Nadler told Fierce Healthcare. Verified U.S. clinicians consulted OpenEvidence 45 million times in October alone, he said.

AI has integrated deeply into specialized medicine as well. There are 300 million physical specialist visits, such as seeing a cardiologist or oncologist, in the U.S. per year. Nadler said OpenEvidence handles about one query from a medical specialist for every patient visit to a medical specialist in America.

Building on its massive adoption with clinicians, the company is now pushing deeper into health systems.

The agreement with NYU Langone builds on OpenEvidence's broader reach in New York. The company already has an enterprise rollout across NewYork-Presbyterian's 10 hospitals and nearly 350 care sites, a health-system-wide deployment at Mount Sinai, and a specialized precision oncology partnership with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. It also has partnerships with leading New York City medical schools around clinical training and research.

A recent large-scale study examined OpenEvidence’s rapid adoption and how clinicians are using AI in the clinic. Nearly 1 million U.S. clinicians submitted 271 million AI-enabled clinical queries through OpenEvidence's platform from January 2024 to June 2026, according to a paper published in JAMA. More than half of the users in the sample (556,200) were physicians, according to researchers from Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. These physicians submitted an average of 37 queries per month of use. Early-career physicians and those in oncology, hematology, internal medicine and family medicine submitted a higher-than-average share of queries, according to the study.

The study found that most of the queries were related to clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management. Diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries.

“Two key takeaways are that an enormous number of physicians are using AI for clinical care and that they are often using it in areas where they don’t have specific expertise,” said corresponding author Anupam Jena, the Joseph P. Newhouse Professor of Health Care Policy in the Blavatnik Institute at HMS and HMS professor of medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

“Everyone appreciates the huge potential for AI to change how medicine is practiced, but right now, we have limited information on how many doctors are using it, what they are using it for, and how it’s impacting patients,” Jena said. The JAMA study tackles the first two of those questions, the researchers noted.

The study also found that monthly active OpenEvidence users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703,265 in June 2026. Queries per active user increased substantially, from 18 per month to 39.5, and month-to-month retention reached roughly 90% in 2026. By June, 92.5% of active users were returning users rather than brief adopters, according to the study.

#5694. The ETS Investment Engine: Scaling Europe’s Strategic E-fuel Market for Shipping & Aviation

Making the ETS a strategic investment tool for aviation and shipping

The EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) review proposal published in July 2026 is intended to make the EU’s most vital climate policy mechanism fit for its 2040 climate targets. It also carries the ambition to turn the ETS into an ‘’engine for innovation and investment”.

This policy brief looks at the investment dimension of the ETS proposal with respect to the aviation and maritime sectors. They are major contributors to the ETS revenue generation. We argue, however, that the proposed framework is not fit for purpose to adequately support clean fuel investments in these hard-to-abate sectors.

The ETS Review is an opportunity to set up a tailor-made investment tool to de-risk and boost the production and uptake of e-fuels, using the ETS funds from aviation and shipping. Early financial support is crucial for the development of a domestic e-fuels value chain, Europe’s geostrategic autonomy and the EU’s industrial position in the global competition for clean technologies. RFNBOs are the most scalable fuels needed to reach the targets under FuelEU Maritime and ReFuelEU Aviation.

#5693. Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule

Labor Department finalizes PBM transparency rule" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has locked in a regulation that will require pharmacy benefit managers to disclose fees and compensation to self-funded employers.

The rule, finalized by the Department of Labor's Employee Benefits Security Administration, aims to ensure that employers can see what drug manufacturers, pharmacies and other entities are paying their PBMs and any affiliated brokers and consultants.

The department said in an announcement that this data will support employers in negotiating contracts and pushing to lower drug costs for their workers and their dependents.

“This is a win for every American worker who has ever paid too much at the pharmacy counter,” said Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling in the announcement. “For years, PBMs have operated in the shadows, pocketing hidden fees while workers and employers were left in the dark."

Under the rule, PBMs must disclose several key sources of compensation, including manufacturer rebates, any compensation when the price for a drug paid by the plan exceeds reimbursement to the pharmacy, and any payments recouped from pharmacies for dispensed drugs.

The rule was first proposed in late January, and while it enjoys support with employer groups, pharmacy benefit managers have pushed back on the changes.

The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying organization for PBMs, in March called for the agency to rescind the proposed rule, as after it was unveiled, lawmakers passed industry reforms as part of a bipartisan health funding package.

Those congressional PBM reforms include multiple provisions around transparency, and PCMA argued that the DOL rule would create duplicative reporting and disclosure requirements for these companies to navigate.

In a statement Thursday, PCMA President David Marin said that the organization is "extremely concerned that it will lead to higher patient costs and less competition, the opposite of the Department’s stated intent."

"The Department has made modest efforts to harmonize the rule with the recently enacted federal law, but we are concerned it may have exceeded Congress’s intent and its own authority," Marin said. "Patients, employers and unions will have no new meaningful transparency from this action, but prescription drug benefits will now be more expensive."

"This could also lead to greater concentration in our industry as smaller PBMs face excessive reporting demands," Marin added.

DOL said in the announcement that the final rule "implements the bipartisan transparency reforms Congress enacted earlier this year." One of the key goals, the agency said, is to better support employers and plan sponsors in meeting their fiduciary duties under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA).

As they face additional pressure on their ERISA compliance, employers cheered the DOL rule and PBM reform more broadly. The ERISA Industry Committee (ERIC) said in a statement that the rule will offer "a clearer view of what their health plans actually pay."

"We applaud the administration for advancing much-needed transparency related to PBMs and affiliated entities," said James Gelfand, CEO of ERIC, in the release. "Large employers pay for their workers’ prescriptions, but many can’t see how much of that money their PBM and any affiliated entity keeps."

"This rule will fill a critical gap in the legislation Congress passed earlier this year, for the first time giving employers a real view into so-called 'spread pricing' arrangements and helping plan sponsors to improve the affordability of prescription drugs for working families," Gelfand said.

#5692. Court rejects CMS' definition of 'medical frailty' under Medicaid work requirements

Court rejects CMS' definition of 'medical frailty' under Medicaid work requirements" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Massachusetts judge has sided with a coalition of states in an ongoing lawsuit over the rollout of Medicaid work requirements, and rejected the Trump administration's definition of "medical frailty" for critical exemptions.

Judge Richard Stearns ruled Thursday that a regulation issued over the summer that aimed to offer guardrails to the implementation of the work requirements unlawfully limited the group of people who would qualify as "medically frail" and would thus be exempted.

In the rule, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said that the frailty exemption would apply when a "physical, mental, or other behavioral health condition significantly impairs the individual’s ability to comply with the community engagement requirement."

This runs afoul of existing law, as there are individuals in five frailty categories established by Congress who may not qualify for the exemption under CMS' definition, Stearns said.

"Because enforcement of an unlawful definition of 'medically frail' may lead to the disenrollment of otherwise eligible vulnerable individuals relying on Medicaid coverage for continuity of care, the States (and public) face potential for great hardship in the absence of an injunction," Stearns wrote. "The court accordingly will issue the permanent injunction requested by the States."

Stearns' ruling isn't a complete win for the state plaintiffs, as he allowed other challenged provisions to stand. Under the order, he determined that CMS should offer states a six-month stay of enforcement on frailty determinations given the short timeline ahead of the work requirements' rollout.

States are down to the wire in implementing the requirements, which were established as part of the massive H.R. 1 legislation in the summer of 2025. The eligibility determinations must be in place nationally on Jan. 1, and experts have warned that the added administrative burden is likely to lead millions to fall out of the Medicaid coverage rolls.

A federal judge has rejected a request from 26 states for a preliminary injunction in the Trump administration's rollout of work requirements in Medicaid.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized implementation guidelines for states in June, with the eligibility requirements set to take effect on Jan. 1. States have until Aug. 31 to communicate with enrollees about the impacts of the changes.

In the lawsuit, the states argued that they do not have the resources necessary to meet the timelines that CMS established in June. They also pushed back on multiple provisions of the final rule, including regulators ultimate definition of medical frailty, which will have a significant impact on who qualifies for exemptions to the requirements.

In an order issued Wednesday, Massachusetts District Judge Richard Stearns wrote that the states did not prove that establishing the systems necessary to make the eligibility determinations would cause them irreparable harm, as CMS said it would reimburse them for 90% of the costs for setting up those mechanisms.

However, he said that the order does not reflect the court's opinion on the merits of the broader litigation, which challenge provisions of the rule under the Administrative Procedure Act. Making a determination on that, as it questions whether officials hewed closely to Congressional intent in regulating the rollout of the requirements, requires a more complete picture.

"These are determinations that, in the view of the court, should be made on a developed record of the kind that informs a court’s decision at the summary judgment stage of a case," wrote Stearns.

A coalition of 26 states is suing the Trump administration over its rollout of Medicaid work requirements.

In the lawsuit—jointly led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell, and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport—the states seek to challenge provisions in the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services' recently-finalized rule establishing guardrails for the work requirements implementation.

A key pillar of that rule is the agency's definition of who would be considered "medically frail," and thus qualify for an exemption to the requirements. The states argue that the newly established definition will make it far harder for people who may need an exemption to obtain one.

In addition, under the rule, states are now asked to notify Medicaid enrollees of the incoming work requirements by Aug. 31, though the requirements will not be in place until Jan. 1. The suing states argue that this new window leaves them with insufficient time to reach out to members.

The lawsuit is asking the courts to block or strike down these parts of the rule, as they have already made strides toward implementing the work requirements based on previous CMS guidance and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which established the national mandate for the eligibility requirements.

If states fail to comply with the final rule, they face significant potential fines, the suing states said.

In a press release from Massachusetts Attorney General Campbell's office, the state notes that officials raised concerns with CMS about the impact of sudden changes to the timeline, which could lead to disruptions in implementation.

In addition, the states argue that the work requirements violate the Administrative Procedure Act, as there is "substantial" evidence that the administrative barriers can lead people who are eligible to lose coverage given the burden in keeping up with the requirements.

“The Trump Administration’s attempt to impose new, burdensome requirements on Medicaid recipients threatens access to healthcare for our most vulnerable residents and families,” said Campbell in a press release. “Congress made clear that people with serious medical conditions should not lose coverage. We are asking the court to block these unlawful provisions to protect Medicaid recipients and prevent needless strain on Massachusetts’ healthcare system.”

Beyond California, Massachusetts and New Jersey, other states signed on to the lawsuit include Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Hawaii, Illinois, Kentucky, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington and Wisconsin.

#5691. BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials

BCBSMA, Medzown team up to match members with clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts is teaming up with precision medicine company Medzown to make it easier for members with complex conditions to participate in clinical trials.

In the partnership, Medzown's tech stack will identify the members that are most likely to benefit from a novel therapy for their condition, and then match them with potential clinical trials. The company will then deploy a team of scientists, clinical trial experts and care navigators to work alongside the patient and their care team through the process.

Jennifer Levin Carter, M.D., the CEO of Medzown, told Fierce Healthcare that there's no shortage of new drugs and therapies coming through the pipeline for complex diseases like cancer, but access is a significant challenge.

"The next frontier for precision medicine is making sure that the right patient can actually get access," Carter said.

BCBSMA will notify members of their eligibility for the program, and participation is voluntary. The program is offered at no additional cost for members.

Karl Laskowski, M.D., vice president for clinical programs and strategy at BCBSMA, said in an interview that complex diseases like cancer are often scary and difficult for patients to navigate, and clinical trials offer access to therapies or care they "wouldn’t have otherwise at their disposal."

"It is not always clear what to do, and there’s a lot coming at you," he said. "We want to show up as a trusted ally, making sure that we are filling a need there for people to get advice, taking advantage of whatever may be the most appropriate."

The insurer said that the partnership with Medzown builds on its existing work to manage complex diseases. For example, in June, BCBSMA entered a value-based care contract with Thyme Care, offering its services as an extension of the patient's current care team.

It's BCBSMA's first specialty-specific value-based care relationship, the insurer said.

Laskowski said that it's early days for the partnership with Medzown, but the team is gathering feedback on what's working and what's not to continue improving and building on this foundation.

Carter echoed the sentiment, saying that while there's likely "tremendous opportunity" to grow from here, the focus is on making sure the current program is functioning at the highest level for the members it serves.

She added that the Medzown team believes that a precision medicine data layer will be critical to healthcare more broadly as the treatment for complex disease becomes more and more personal.

"Treatment of cancer has totally changed for many cancer types," she said. "It has turned into a disease that can be managed on a long-term and chronic basis."

"We need to be able to integrate that ... so that these great and fabulous new esoteric therapies get into the continuum of care," Carter said.

The for-profit this week reported $5.63 billion in net operating revenues for the quarter, not counting $646 million in contract termination revenue tied to its divorce with CommonSpirit Health that was recognized during the quarter. The tally was 6.5% above the same period last year and above the $5.47 billion consensus estimate, per Zacks Investment Research.

The bigger standouts were its $6.64 adjusted earnings per share, well above the prior year’s $3.70 earnings per share and more than 40% above the consensus estimate of $4.60 per share. Further, executives highlighted third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $1.36 billion (about 16% above the street, per Stephens), about 10% year-over-year growth when excluding $147 million in one-time items stemming from the shifting timing of its CommonSpirit contract winddown.

Based on those results, the health system boosted 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance by $195 million, building on the prior increase issued during the summer. CEO Saum Sutaria, M.D., told analysts during a Thursday morning call that the change “is supported by our continued expectations for strong fundamental performance as well as the one-time items in the back half of the year. Notably, over 40% of our total guidance increase for this year is from fundamental outperformance.”

For the quarter, executives generally described rising hospital activity and continued expense reductions that outpaced industry-wide weak surgical volumes and payer mix challenges.

Specifically, same-hospital admissions rose 2.8% year over year, adjusted admissions rose 3.2% and hospital surgeries dipped 1.1%. Net hospital revenues rose 6.1% year over year while revenue per adjusted admission rose a narrower 0.2%, as “continued pricing strength” and volumes outpaced 18% declines in exchange admissions and revenues, executives said.

Adjusted EBITDA for the hospitals business grew from last year’s $607 million to $818 million (including the $147 million one-time items). The segment also recognized $32 million more in favorable pre-tax impact tied to supplemental Medicaid payments compared to the prior year, or $356 million in total.

In Tenet’s high-margin ambulatory segment, same-facility net patient service revenues rose 4.5% year over year despite a 1.5% drop in same-facility cases. Same-facility net revenue per case rose 6.1%, which executives said reflects the company’s ongoing strategic push to capture high-acuity patients. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.1% year over year to $537 million.

On surgical numbers, which have been a sore spot for systems over the last few months, Sutaria said the company was pleased that both sides of the business were performing “generally consistent or better than we’re seeing in the general industry. … I would not say this is a gangbusters surgical environment right now.”

The ambulatory surgery market in particular has been heating up as health systems look to flesh out their networks and meet the calls for care in lower-cost settings. Sutaria, in response to an analyst question, acknowledged this week’s news that Bon Secours Mercy Health would be acquiring Surgery Partners in a $5.7 billion deal. Taken alongside the summer’s $3.9 billion AmSurg close by Ascension, he said that Tenet’s platform remains the standout for differentiated earnings growth. “Look, in terms of the two recent ASC acquisitions, you know, I personally extended my congratulations to both new owners,” he said. On concerns of dealmaking competition, Sutaria noted that the company was “very successful” in new ASC acquisitions during the quarter and that “the vast majority of which were not competitive processes, but came exclusively to [us] in those processes.”

As for next year, executives said Tenet is expected to grow its overall EBITDA. That’s after excluding the impacts of the CommonSpirit contract termination, and taking into account “the current known regulatory frameworks” such as those outlining Medicaid work requirements and supplemental payments.

#5689. Study Strengthens Case for Stent-Free PCI in De Novo Coronary Lesions

— Magic Touch drug-coated balloon was noninferior to drug-eluting stent

For de novo coronary lesions, drug-coated balloons (DCBs) were just as effective as standard drug-eluting stents, the TRANSFORM II trial showed.

Among patients with native coronary lesions undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), the incidence of target lesion failure at 12 months -- including cardiac death, target vessel myocardial infarction (MI), and ischemia-driven target lesion revascularization -- was 2.1% with the Magic Touch sirolimus DCB and 2.4% with standard everolimus drug-eluting stents (DES; HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.47-1.59).

The DCB thus met prespecified criteria for noninferiority (P=0.004), reported Bernardo Cortese, MD, MSc, of Fondazione Ricerca e Innovazione Cardiovascolare in Milan, at the Transcatheter Cardiovascular Therapeutics annual conference hosted by the Cardiovascular Research Foundation.

"All of this put into the context of the available literature and the SELUTION De Novo clinical trial, I can conclude that the DCB approach is a safe and effective alternative to stents in a selected population of de novo lesions, but bear in mind that there is no class effect for drug-coated balloons," Cortese said.

The Magic Touch is a DCB designed to release sirolimus and have it stay in the arterial wall for 8 to 12 weeks. The appeal of a DCB is that, unlike DES, the standard of care for native coronary artery disease, no permanent metal is left behind during PCI.

DCBs are already established as a treatment for coronary in-stent restenosis, an indication for which paclitaxel- (the Agent DCB) and sirolimus-eluting DCB models (the Selution SLR) are available on the market. The evidence is more shaky for DCBs in native coronary artery disease, especially following the negative REC-CAGEFREE I trial, though in last year's SELUTION De Novo trial, the Selution DCB was shown to be noninferior to DES for rates of target lesion failure.

Of note, though rates of clinically driven target lesion revascularization were comparable between groups in TRANSFORM II, rates of any target lesion revascularization were higher in the DCB group (2.5% vs 1.1%, HR 2.31, 95% CI 1.10-4.85).

One theory, noted Cortese, is that physicians in this open-label trial may have tended to re-treat patients if they had subpar angiographic results after DCB therapy, whereas they may have been more conservative if they saw stents in the picture. "But the numbers were very low, so this is very, very speculative," he cautioned.

Besides the concern for target lesion revascularization, there is also the question of costs.

Session co-chair Ajay Kirtane, MD, of NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center in New York City, questioned if cath labs will be willing to switch to DCBs if the listing prices are about $6,000, compared with the $300 to $400 for DES.

"Financial reimbursements are still a big issue for centers, and I think it will continue to be, and particularly as we get farther along, and all the Medicare mandates end. So I think we'll have to wait and see," said panelist Jennifer Tremmel, MD, of Stanford University Medical Center in Palo Alto, California. "We're going to have to decide who gets DCB, who gets DES, when do they get it, and the financials are going to make a difference. So I'm curious to see how things go over the long term, and ultimately which patients we decide to use this in first."

TRANSFORM II was an open-label multicenter trial conducted in Europe, Asia, and Brazil. Participants had to have native coronary lesions with reference vessel diameters measuring 2.0 to 3.5 mm and lesion lengths no greater than 50 mm.

Following successful vessel preparation, patients were randomized 1:1 to the Magic Touch sirolimus DCB or the everolimus DES. Out of 2,699 people screened, 2,223 met criteria for entry, and 1,842 had successful lesion preparation and were ultimately randomized.

Mean age was about 63 years, and most patients were men. Initial presentation was roughly split between acute coronary syndrome and chronic coronary syndrome. Over 35% had diabetes, and about one in three had a prior MI. Approximately 30% had a high bleeding risk.

Lesions were type B2/C in about two in three cases. Bailout stenting was required in 7.6% of the DCB group.

Cortese reported that the minimum lumen diameter at baseline was about 0.92 mm, and in-device acute lumen gain averaged 0.76 mm with DCB and 1.30 mm with DES. On quantitative coronary angiography, the percent diameter stenosis at baseline was about 59%, and this dropped to 31% after lesion preparation. After PCI, the in-device percent diameter stenosis was 26.8% with DCB and 12.3% with DES. The proportion of patients with in-device residual stenosis <30% was 61.2% with DCB and 97.9% with DES.

Regarding the primary endpoint, intention-to-treat results were consistent with the per-protocol analysis, according to Cortese. Individual components of target lesion failure were also generally favorable with DCB:

A secondary endpoint, net adverse clinical events (all-cause mortality, any MI, ischemic stroke, or major bleeding), was not significantly different between the DCB and DES arms (4.1% vs 5.3%, HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.50-1.17).

Cortese stressed that these results do not apply to lesions with unsuccessful lesion preparation and excluded groups (patients with severe calcification, highly tortuous vessels, and left main or vein graft lesions; ST-segment elevation MI within 48 hours; previous PCI in the target vessel; complex bifurcation lesions; and ejection fractions below 30%, among others).

Among other study limitations, event rates were much lower than expected, and the results may have limited generalizability given that the operators were all from experienced DCB centers.

As for the question of whether DCBs might eventually reach superiority over DES for native coronary lesions, Cortese said this will require long-term data, and his group does plan to continue patient follow-up out to 5 years.

"We are expecting to see fewer events starting from year 3, like we have seen with paclitaxel-coated balloons in a patient-level meta-analysis," he said.

#5688. Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027

Community Health Systems logs $86M net loss in Q3, hopes for return of 'pent-up' electives in 2027" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A “challenging macro environment” serving up more uninsured patients and fewer commercial elective procedures dragged Community Health Systems below internal and analyst operating forecasts for the third quarter.

The 59-hospital system reported $2.76 billion in third-quarter net operating revenue, down about 10.7% year over year due to several divestments but up 3.8% on a same-store basis. Net loss was $86 million, -$0.63 per diluted share or -$0.48 after adjustment, compared to the prior year’s $1.27 per share net income.

The consensus estimates for revenue and earnings were $2.78 billion and -$0.22 per diluted share, per Zach’s Investment Research. The company’s shares were trading over 10% below the open late Thursday afternoon.

“While overall financial results fell below our internal forecast, due to the same factors that many peers are experiencing—namely elevated uninsured volumes and temporary softness in commercial elective procedures—we delivered sequential volume gains and solid cash flow performance,” CEO Kevin Hammons summarized Thursday morning on the company’s earnings call. “Importantly, our leading indicators clearly demonstrate that care is being deferred rather than lost to competitors.”

CHS has reduced its 2026 guidance ranges for net operating revenues, adjusted EBITDA and cash ranges.

Same-store admissions rose 2.2% while adjusted admissions increased 3.6% year over year. However, about half of the adjusted admissions growth was among uninsured patients, Chief Financial Officer Jason Johnson explained, and a 2% overall increase in same-store surgeries masked low numbers for commercial electives. These factors held same-store net revenue per adjusted admission to just 0.2% year-over-year growth.

Executives, in response to analyst questions, noted that the 2% increase is a clear improvement from recent quarters’ declines.

“We saw more cardiac procedures and more GI procedures this quarter,” Hammons explained. “The cardiac procedures, though, … are low margin because of the high cost of the devices. What we were short on were the elective orthopedic and elective general surgery-type procedures that are higher-margin business, and those are more elective type procedures. […] Again, kind of fits back into the story of we believe this is a patient decision around care, and being influenced by financial decisions.”

In the meantime, Hammons said the company is “proactively managing our cost structure,” yielding more than $100 million in projected annual savings so far “without compromising our clinical capacity or operational readiness for tomorrow” when those electives return.

Looking to the tea leaves in 2027, executives suggested there would be a “modest” headwind from Medicaid work requirements. While more than half of the company’s Medicaid volumes are in expansion states, “we think it’s likely that the very large majority will qualify for continued coverage under the various exemptions like age, caregiver status or medical frailty, but we really just don’t know exactly what the impact will be until the data starts coming in,” Johnson said during the call.

Exchange volume reductions due to coverage drop-offs could see “some potential future degradation” based on how open enrollment goes, he said, although “we think there will be a modest headwind there.” Provider tax cuts will also likely bring another “modest” hit, while medical specialty fees expected to grow “well above inflation” are “the big question mark on cost,” Johnson added.

On the other hand, executives counted payment rate updates, investments in outpatient and ambulatory locations, expense management and $25 million to $30 million in year-one funds from the Rural Health Transformation Program as positive factors for 2027 earnings.

Further, they suggested that this year’s “uncharacteristic” dearth in elective procedures could come to an end as cost-conscious patients—who are still captured in CHS’ care networks—eventually book their deferred care.

“There’s pent-up demand,” Hammons said. “Ultimately, we think that it comes back into the system because when you need a joint replacement, it’s not going to heal on its own.”

“Our initial expectations [were that when] we got into the back half of this year, we would see that seasonality growth. We did not see as much of that in the third quarter as we had previously expected,” he explained. “As you get to October, if people have not met their co-pay and deductible, it’s likely they could push that off until next year, get their procedures in the first half of the year and have a longer period of time to have other medical procedures done without having to pay a co-pay and deductible again. So we’ve adjusted our guidance accordingly to reflect our outlook on that.”

CHS is hardly alone in navigating surgery and payer mix challenges. Fellow for-profits HCA Healthcare, Universal Health Services and Tenet Healthcare each described varying levels of impact during earnings calls held this week. Each held off from detailing concrete estimates for the coming year, noting a need to monitor year-end trends and the exchanges’ open enrollment period, but acknowledged that Medicaid coverage will likely continue to be a sore spot.
