#5687. Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates

Teladoc Health beats Q3 expectations as BetterHelp insurance growth accelerates" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Teladoc Health raised its 2026 outlook after better-than-expected third-quarter results, as BetterHelp’s insurance pivot gained traction and Integrated Care profitability improved.

The virtual care company posted declining revenue but still beat Wall Street on both revenue and profit. Teladoc Health's Q3 beat drove shares up nearly 27% Thursday after the company reported Q3 earnings Wednesday after market close.

Teladoc Health faces near-term pressure as it transitions its virtual mental health business, BetterHelp, from a cash pay model to an in-network, insurance-covered model.

The company's consolidated revenue was $605.1 million, down 3.4% year-over-year but towards the high end of management's guidance range, as solid performance in the integrated care business and strong BetterHelp insurance growth was partially offset by ongoing headwinds in BetterHelp’s cash pay revenue, Chief Financial Officer Michael Grasher, who joined the company in August, told investors and analysts on the company's Q3 earnings call Wednesday. Teladoc's Q3 revenue exceeded the $588.4 million analyst consensus.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted EBITDA of $79.4 million, up roughly 14% year-over-year and compared to the $67.7 million consensus target. Teladoc reported a net loss of $26.9 million, or a loss per share of 15 cents, versus Street expectations for a loss of 22 cents per share.

The company generated $79 million in free cash flow in the third quarter, and it ended the quarter with $850 million in cash and cash equivalents.

Teladoc Health raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $2.39 billion to $2.44 billion, raising the midpoint of its full-year 2026 revenue outlook by $13 million, “driven largely by the updated BetterHelp outlook,” Grasher said.

The company expects adjusted EBITDA of $277 million to $303 million, up $3 million at the midpoint versus the prior range.

Teladoc Health is focused on expanding access to its direct-to-consumer virtual mental health services, BetterHelp, through insurance coverage while also growing its integrated care enterprise business.

"As we consider the market more broadly as a company, we continue to see opportunities for virtual care to play an increasing role in addressing key challenges in healthcare," Teladoc Health CEO Chuck Divita said during the call.

As a scaled virtual care company, Teladoc's technology and services help address rising healthcare costs, expand access, improve chronic disease and mental health care and ease pressure on providers and the broader healthcare system, Divita said.

The BetterHelp segment brought in $207 million in revenue, down 13% year-over-year. BetterHelp commercial insurance revenue exceeded expectations, coming in at $32.1 million, up from $3.7 million a year ago and beating management's forecast of $25 million to $31 million. BetterHelp cash-pay revenue declined 25% to $174 million in Q3, as fewer users paid out of pocket. But cash pay performance for BetterHelp was "better than anticipated," Divita said. The company continues to reduce advertising spend for the BetterHelp business while also "adapting its advertising and marketing approach to reflect insurance priorities," he noted.

BetterHelp's pivot to an in-network insurance model is gaining momentum with 27,000 covered sessions per week in Q3, an annualized run rate above $140 million and more than 11,000 credentialed therapists, Divita told analysts and investors. That compares to the $110 million annualized run rate from weekly sessions referenced in Teladoc's second-quarter earnings call.

In Q3, 36% of acquired U.S. users came from insurance, up about 8 percentage points from the second quarter, according to executives. The company added more than 3,000 therapists to the network during the quarter.

"We believe expanding insurance access can help create a more durable position for BetterHelp over time," Divita said.

The company expects continued growth in 2027 as it expands provider capacity, improves therapist engagement and grows utilization of BetterHelp’s services, Grasher said.

Teladoc is targeting a $200 million annualized BetterHelp insurance run rate by the end of 2027.

“While there is more work ahead, this was a solid quarter driven by execution, and continued progress across our key strategic priorities,” Grasher said.

Teladoc Health continues to invest in its core business, integrated care, which brought in $399 million in Q3 revenue, up 2% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA of $74.9 million, up 13% year-over-year. Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 18.8%, and Grasher noted on the call that the Q3 margin expansion occurred despite the ongoing mix shift toward visit-based arrangements.

The virtual company is focused on moving health plan and employer clients away from fragmented point solutions to its broader Teladoc One model. Teladoc One, unveiled in July, is designed to offer a more coordinated, personalized approach for members, while tying payment to clinical and financial outcomes, executives said. As part of the model, Teladoc Health care teams deliver and coordinate care across virtual settings and in partnership with a member's local providers.

The company has moved forward with initial launch partners for Teladoc One, and the platform will be more broadly available in 2027, executives said.

"We are encouraged by the level of client engagement and member feedback on Teladoc One at this point, reinforcing our view that clients are looking for solutions that can deliver a more connected experience, address more care needs, and demonstrate greater accountability for outcomes and impact," Divita said.

Outside the U.S. market, Teladoc Health developed a "hybrid care" model that combines its technology with virtual clinical services delivered into physical healthcare settings. The company sees opportunities to build out that model with U.S. hospitals and health systems. To support that strategy, Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, a company that provides virtual clinical services to U.S. hospitals and health systems. Teledigm partners with hospitals and clinics to deliver remote acute, outpatient and specialty care.

Financial details of the Teledigm Health deal were not disclosed.

"We believe the market dynamics supporting the adoption of our hybrid care models in other countries are also increasingly prevalent with hospitals and health systems in the U.S., including healthcare workforce and capacity challenges, financial pressures and the need to improve access for underserved and rural communities. As a result, we see an opportunity to leverage our experience in hybrid care within the U.S. to support future growth," Divita said during the call.

"This is a company that we've worked with for a long time that's used our technology and really commercialized the services part of the equation using our technology. The tracks have been laid in terms of using our technology and support and use cases to those health systems. We think bringing that expertise we have in non-U.S. markets, which is considerable and has been a nice source of growth for us, bringing that expertise combined with our technology and telehealth services together, we can really go after that market opportunity in 2027," he told investors and analysts during a Q&A on the earnings call.

Teladoc also continues to invest in product innovation to support its integrated care business. The company expanded its Solo enterprise platform with two AI tools designed to add clinical capabilities without forcing hospitals to adopt more standalone technology. The two new capabilities—dubbed SoloVitals and SoloScribe—bring contact-free vital sign measurement and ambient clinical documentation directly into clinical workflows.

Wall Street analysts saw positive signs of progress in the turnaround of Teladoc's BetterHelp business in the latest quarter.

Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Teladoc's third-quarter results provided a positive update on the company’s ability to convert strong insurance demand into revenue.

"We continue to view BetterHelp’s transition toward greater in-network coverage as the key driver of business stabilization, particularly as insurance growth increasingly offsets cash-pay declines and added capacity of credentialed therapists enables the company to capture strong underlying demand," Daniels wrote in an analyst note.

"We are also encouraged by the company’s continued 2026 product introductions and launches across virtual care, including implementing Teladoc One with early launch partners and expanding hybrid care and AI-enabled solutions set to support continued growth in the Integrated Care segment," Daniels wrote.

However, ongoing weakness in BetterHelp’s cash-pay business "is likely to weigh on overall segment performance and temper the pace of the company’s broader turnaround," Daniels noted.

Teladoc remains in a transitional phase, Daniels noted, "navigating slower growth and a challenging end-market, with increased emphasis on profitability, product enhancements and capital deployment into new growth avenues."

#5686. New Florida ‘Agrihood’ Development Bets on Organic Farming to Lure Homebuyers

A new masterplanned community in Northeast Florida will offer multiple organic farms to attract buyers who are more interested in fresh vegetables than the state's famed beaches.

Saratoga Springs, a new development from Freehold Communities, will eventually have about 4,500 homes within multiple communities on 2,400 acres of land.

Located in Green Cove Springs, outside of Jacksonville, the "agrihood" will contain numerous working farms, bringing sustainable agriculture, farm-to-table dining, farmers' markets, and all things farm-related to the community.

Agrihoods, which mix subdivision developments with agriculture, most often appear in communities with large, undeveloped tracts of land or existing agricultural zoning.

This combination of agricultural land and neighborhood must then be developed to include housing while still incorporating an agricultural component of the community, according to Freehold Communities.

The first phase of the Saratoga Springs agrihood—a 55-plus community called Sagebrooke—began sales in August 2026.

The gated senior community is built by Ryan Homes, with eight single-family home designs ranging from 1,488 to 2,729 square feet.

The active adult community will contain the usual amenities—such as a resort-style pool and pickleball, tennis, bocce courts and a putting green—but also boasts a private working farm and vineyard, a farm share from harvested crops, and a farm store.

Here, the signature crop will be a muscadine vineyard featuring Florida’s native grape, which thrives in the heat and humidity.

Home prices in the development range from $349,990 to $556,990. A spokesperson for Freehold wouldn't reveal the number of sales thus far but says that "it's exciting to see the level of demand."

Carmen Eldridge, 40, cofounder with her husband, Tripp, of Convivial Foodscapes, is heading up the farm aspect of Saratoga Springs. The couple led farm planning on two other Freehold agrihoods—Arden, in Palm Beach County; and Carnes Crossroads in Goose Creek, SC.

The pair navigate the process for creating functional agrihoods—everything from vetting land purchases, to business planning and budgets, to irrigation needs, to farm design and infrastructure construction, as well as distribution models for getting the produce into the wider community.

"It's a movement that is catching on," she says of agrihoods.

According to an Urban Land Institute study, agrihoods are a growing trend, available in at least 27 states. Key agrihood features include conservation space, protected farmland, farm stands and markets, and edible landscaping.

"People are drawn to the idea of living closer to where their food comes from," says Eldridge. "They like the wide open green spaces, and are into healthy eating and longevity."

"It's more appealing to live near an organic farm than a golf course," she adds, noting that a lot of parents want their children to know that "a carrot comes out of the ground, not from a bag in the grocery store."

The Saratoga Springs farms will be cultivated by professional farmers—not the residents. But residents will be able to pick or bring home farm produce round the clock, a perk included in the HOA fees. (They will not have private plots or gardens.)

Eldridge tells Realtor.com that her agrihood consultancy has been in brisk demand as sustainable farms become the latest trend in the masterplanned community world. But she asserts that farms go far beyond typical amenities such a pool, fitness center, or pickleball courts.

"A farm is social infrastructure, it's not just an amenity," she says. "It creates repeated, meaningful touch points between neighbors. A farm actively builds a community identity in a way that other amenities can’t replicate. That’s why it’s catching more attention now."

She counts Freehold as among the leaders in the agrihood trend.

"Some developers want to put in a community garden to check the box, like, got the dog park, got the pool, got the community garden, check," she says. "But they go all-in and do it really well."

Eldridge says farming is in her blood, as her maternal immigrant grandparents had been farmers in Spain.

"At the time, everyone was a farmer," she says. "There were no grocery stores. You farmed or you died."

She grew up with plenty of fresh produce from her family's backyard gardens.

"I didn't think much of it at the time," she says. "I was just told to go out back and pick some green beans for dinner."

When she informed her grandparents that she was going to study organic crop production in college, they weren't too pleased.

"They said, 'We moved here so you didn't have to be a farmer!'"

After graduating from the University of Florida with a degree in Political Science, focusing on Agriculture Policy and Organic and Sustainable Crop Production, Eldridge served as a Sustainable Agriculture Peace Corps volunteer in Panama, then founded a teaching farm at the University of North Florida.

Eventually, she and husband, Tripp, worked to set up the farms at Freehold's Arden agrihood, where they served as farm directors for five years; then they designed and built the farm at Carnes Crossroads.

The pair, who jokingly refer to themselves as "landless farmers," formed Convivial Foodscapes in 2020, and soon afterward came aboard the Saratoga Springs project.

Agrihoods, and the employment of local farmers to work the land, have been somewhat of an unexpected and steady income source for those in the notoriously difficult farming industry.

Farmers from the vicinity are also invited into the private community to sell produce and goods, offering a larger customer base for those who work the land on tight margins.

"Our farmer population is aging," she says, noting that agrihoods offer "a job for farmers with a living wage and health benefits."

Eldridge, who uses only organic farming techniques, takes great joy in people's reactions to fresh produce.

"I love when people's faces light up when they learn what a real tomato actually tastes like," she says. "I live for those moments."

But what most excites Eldrige about the concept of agrihoods and their growing popularity is the social aspects.

Farms offer diverse ways for communities to connect through food—picking produce, volunteering, helping to farm, attending workshops, hosting farm-to-table meals, or mingling at special events tied to fresh food or signature crops.

Eldridge, who often attends model home showings at Saratoga Springs, says that the buyer pool is very broad—everyone from young families to downsizing retirees—but they often have one thing in common: they are foodies at heart.

"There is something universally appealing about food," she says. "We all like to eat and we all have a food story."

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. Her work can be found in news outlets worldwide, including Yahoo, SF Gate, New York Post, Seattle-Post Intelligencer, Marie Claire, She Knows, Huffington Post, and New York Magazine. She has an M.A. in journalism from Columbia University. In her spare time, she writes psychological thrillers under a pen name. She lives in Brooklyn, and her cat foster Instagram account has over 4 million views.

#5685. Novel Therapy Lands Speedy Approval for Wart-Like Airway Disease

— Plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy reduced surgery need in recurrent respiratory papillomatosis

The FDA granted accelerated approval to doruxapapogene ralaplasmid and lalikinogene sifuplasmid (Voceryq) to reduce the frequency of surgical papilloma excisions in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP), the agency announced late on Friday.

As the first FDA-approved recombinant plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid targets the wart-like growths that characterize RRP. The growths are caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) and develop in the airways, particularly around the larynx. Severe cases of the rare disease can spread into the respiratory tract and make breathing difficult. There is no cure, but repeated surgeries can remove growths if they return.

FDA based its decision on efficacy data from RRP-001, a phase I/II clinical trial. The open-label trial included 32 patients who'd undergone at least two surgeries in the prior year to remove RRP growths. Among 26 patients who had at least three surgeries in the 12 months before treatment, 27% had a complete response to the plasmid therapy, defined as requiring no surgical excisions during 12 months of follow-up.

"The approval of Voceryq is an important step in improving the quality of life for RRP patients as every surgery carries the risk of laryngeal injury," said investigator Simon Best, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, in a statement from manufacturer Inovio Pharmaceuticals. "I believe it is in the best interest of RRP patients that the standard of care quickly transition away from surgical interventions to immunotherapy after RRP is diagnosed."

Doruxapapogene ralaplasmid-lalikinogene sifuplasmid includes two plasmids that contain genetic coding for HPV proteins and interleukin 12. Patients' own healthy cells transcribe that coding to stimulate immune system attacks against cells infected with the HPV types 6 and 11 that cause RRP.

The therapy's treatment regimen begins with surgical debulking of visible papilloma, followed by an intramuscular dose of the plasmid therapy every 3 weeks for a total of four doses. Label warnings include potential adverse events (AEs) such as muscle contractions, transient bleeding, and vasovagal reactions. The most common AEs in trials included injection site reactions, headache, fatigue, hypertension, nausea, and dizziness.

The new treatment was approved in combination with a proprietary DNA medicine delivery device (CELLECTRA 5PSP). Postmarketing trials will be required to verify and describe the therapy's clinical benefit.

The FDA approved the immunotherapy zopapogene imadenovec (Papzimeos) for RRP in 2025, the first approved medical therapy for the condition.

#5684. Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare

Industry Voices—The other AI divide is already opening in healthcare" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The debate over AI and inequality has largely focused on people—who will have access to the technology, who will benefit from it and who risks being left behind. But inside healthcare, another AI divide is already taking shape. This one is between the hospitals that have the money, talent and infrastructure to put AI to work and those that don't.

The numbers are striking. According to federal data on hospital AI adoption, 71% of U.S. hospitals used predictive AI integrated with their electronic health records in 2024. But adoption reached 96% among large hospitals compared with just 59% among small hospitals. Among hospitals belonging to multi-hospital systems, 86% used predictive AI. Among independent hospitals, it was only 37%.

That gap matters because AI is quickly becoming part of how hospitals survive, not simply an innovation project. The same federal data show some of the fastest-growing hospital AI applications are decidedly practical, including billing and scheduling. These are exactly the kinds of labor-intensive functions where financially stressed hospitals need to find efficiencies.

Yet those hospitals may be the least equipped to make the investment.

Hospitals remain extraordinarily dependent on people to operate. According to the American Hospital Association, workforce spending accounted for about 60% of hospital expenses in 2025, exceeding $1 trillion. Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% that year, more than twice the growth in hospital prices.

This creates a dangerous catch-22. The hospitals with the greatest need to use technology to redesign labor-intensive operations frequently have the least capacity to invest in doing so.

A large health system can afford an AI pilot that fails. It can hire an innovation team, absorb a lengthy implementation, build governance and compliance infrastructure, and try again if the economics don't work. A safety-net, community or independent hospital often has far less room for error. A multi-year software contract that might eventually produce savings still requires money today.

And buying the technology is only the beginning.

Successful AI deployment requires workflow redesign, change management, integration, measurement and governance. Even among hospitals already using predictive AI, the federal data show meaningful variation in how comprehensively models are evaluated for accuracy, bias and performance after implementation. Smaller, rural and independent hospitals also continue to lag their larger counterparts in adoption.

If we leave the market to work this out one hospital at a time, we should expect that divide to compound. Systems that successfully automate expensive workflows can reinvest those savings into their next technology investment. They build institutional knowledge. Their employees get better at implementation. They become more attractive partners to technology companies looking for sophisticated customers and proving grounds.

The hospitals that wait don't simply remain where they are. They lose ground. The answer cannot be telling every hospital to develop a better AI strategy. We need to change the ownership and financing model for healthcare AI.

Hospitals already know how to collaborate when acting collectively creates an advantage. Group purchasing organizations allow them to aggregate purchasing power rather than negotiate for every product independently. Clinical research networks allow institutions to pool patients, expertise and infrastructure to answer questions no single organization could address as effectively alone.

We should apply the same instinct to AI. Instead of requiring every health system to independently buy, implement and govern variations of the same technology, health systems should increasingly pool their purchasing power, operational expertise and capital to build common AI capabilities. And smaller, independent and safety-net organizations need a path into those collaborations rather than simply another vendor contract.

The venture community has a responsibility here as well. We need financing structures that acknowledge the economic reality of the organizations that really need to adopt technologies. That could mean performance-based models where payment is tied to verified savings rather than large upfront commitments. It could mean consortium models in which multiple health systems share implementation resources and governance.

And increasingly, it should mean giving health systems ownership in the companies and infrastructure they help create. Ownership matters because the economics of AI are changing quickly. As the technology itself becomes increasingly commoditized, enduring value will come from distribution, proprietary workflows, real-world implementation knowledge and access to the environments where healthcare actually happens. Health systems contribute enormously to each of those things. Under the traditional vendor model, however, they can provide the workflows, clinical expertise and proving ground and then pay someone else an annual fee for the resulting product.

That bargain deserves to be reconsidered. Collective ownership can help address the trust problem, too. AI adoption isn't only a technology decision. It requires decisions about validation, monitoring, clinical safety and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Federal researchers found that hospitals increasingly rely on multiple parties to evaluate AI, with 74% reporting more than one entity accountable for evaluation. Smaller hospitals should not each have to recreate that infrastructure from scratch.

Shared infrastructure could include common validation standards, clinical oversight, monitoring and implementation expertise. That would give more hospitals access not only to AI, but to the capabilities required to deploy it responsibly.

None of this means every hospital needs to own every AI company, or that traditional vendors disappear. It means we should stop assuming that the only scalable model for healthcare innovation is one technology company selling essentially the same capability to thousands of hospitals one contract at a time.

The AI divide between hospitals is already here. If adoption continues to depend primarily on the size of an organization's balance sheet, the institutions best positioned today will keep accumulating advantages while those with the least room for error fall further behind.

AI gives hospitals a real opportunity to break their dependence on increasingly expensive, labor-intensive ways of operating. But the organizations that need that opportunity most cannot be the last ones able to afford it. Preventing that outcome will require more than making AI cheaper. It will require giving more health systems the ability to build, govern and share in the technology's value, transforming them.

AI should become something hospitals build together, not another advantage reserved for those that could already afford to move first.

Amanda DeMano is SVP of venture creation at Abundant Venture Partners.

Editor's Note: Abundant Venture Partners is a strategic investor in the makers of certain AI technologies, including SpendRule and Playback Health.

#5683. The health care issues STAT reporters are watching in the midterms

#5682. Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds

Alignment Healthcare lowers 2026 outlook as it navigates cost headwinds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Alignment Healthcare is lowering its guidance for the year as it faces significant headwinds to finish out 2026.

The company said in an earnings report released late Thursday that it now expects to bring in $100 million in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, as well as $5.2 billion in revenue. Total membership is set to be at least 305,000, according to the report.

Alignment reported an $8 million loss in the third quarter, compared to a $3.8 million profit one year ago. Profits were $39.9 million through three quarters, up from $10.3 million across the first nine months of 2025.

Revenue in the third quarter was $1.4 billion, compared to $663.7 million in the prior-year quarter. Revenues through the first nine months of 2026 were $3.9 billion, up from $2.9 billion through three quarters in 2025.

CEO John Kao told investors on the company's earnings call Friday morning that some headwinds Alignment is facing include cost spikes in certain service lines, like catastrophic care and skilled nursing, as well as volatility in claims processing.

Last year, Alignment kicked off an effort to migrate to a comprehensive claims system with the goal of accelerating payment speed, growing automated adjudication rates and enhancing payment integrity. Through that process, once the dust settled on the shift, Alignment found "a notable increase in aggressive provider appeal and disputes in our paid claims data" that also drove up costs, Kao said.

Kao said that the insurer has spent the last several months building out its payment integrity capabilities, as well as deploying additional resources to support clinical best practices to mitigate the variation in outcomes for members.

He said that these investments have driven improvements, particularly in September and into October, but the company is still taking a cautious approach to the end of the year.

"Despite our progress, we are taking a prudent approach to the increased trend seen in Q3 and assume that higher costs in the third quarter will continue to weigh on our results for the remainder of the year," Kao said. "I want to emphasize that the guidance we have provided today is a guidance that we are confident in delivering."

Kao also addressed Alignment's performance in the latest round of star ratings scores. Based on federal data, 25% of its members are in plans with at least four stars in 2027, down from 100% in 2026. That four-star threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments in Medicare Advantage.

He said that six of the company's seven contracts were above four stars, but a 3.5 score on the remaining plan, a core HMO offering in California, dragged down its overall performance.

Kao said that the team is "focused on really getting to the root issues in Stars." Alignment has also sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services over the 2027 calculations.

"That's something that we're going to be underscoring yet again," he said. "This is something that everybody in the company has to focus on ... and we'll get this fixed."

#5681. A Pristine 1950s John Lautner ‘Time Capsule’ Just Listed for $2.1M—and It’s Had Only One Owner

Referred to as the Rosemary and Joseph Baldwin Residence, a John Lautner-designed home seeks a new steward in the trendy Los Angeles neighborhood of Silver Lake.

But what’s even more rare is that this three-bedroom, two-bath property spanning 1,679 square feet has had just one owner. With very few updates, it’s a veritable time capsule.

Tucked into a wooded, hillside setting, Lautner balanced the home on posts anchored by shear walls. This creates a floating effect, made even more dramatic with floor-to-ceiling glass and a wraparound deck. That the home is seamlessly integrated into nature, including redwood-plank siding and skylights that coax in nature light, are two other marvels.

“The house is completely original, minus a tree that was growing through the teak deck in the backyard and that needed to be removed,” says Louis Magnano of Modern California House, who is handling the $2,099,999 listing. “It’s about as original as you can get in 2026.”

This includes the entire kitchen as well as lighting fixtures, mahogany paneling, and terrazzo and parquet flooring. As well, the fireplace is original, and all of the windows, too. Each bedroom’s built-ins are also intact. The living room’s inverted-pyramid ceiling and triangular clerestory windows are also striking.

“It’s completely original, which is very rare for these types of homes in L.A.,” says Magnano.

“They get traded (and) things are done to them when they shouldn’t be. This house doesn’t have that. Whoever is going to purchase this home and be the next steward will need to restore and bring it up to today’s standards but while maintaining the original quality of the home. The sellers want to see it restored.”

This could mean updating the systems, for starters.

How often does a Lautner-designed home hop onto the market, though?

“They have been coming up quite frequently for sale in the last few years,” says Magnano, “but there’s so few and far between, maybe it’s just a special time in the marketplace.”

In 1955, Lautner—a Taliesin Fellow under Frank Lloyd Wright during the 1930s—was commissioned by commercial artist James Baldwin and his wife Rosemary to create their family home, utilizing a 7,491-square-foot lot. Rosemary’s sister introduced them to Lautner.

Lautner’s residence (Silvertop) is on the same street as the Baldwin home.

“Silver Lake is really known for a lot of its architectural history, not only by John Lautner, but Richard Neutra, Rudolph Schinder, to name a few starchitects,” says Magnano.

Lautner would later design three other Southern California homes that put him on the map: The Chemosphere (1960), The Sheats-Goldstein Residence (1961-1963) and The Elrod Residence (1968).

“The Baldwin Residence marks a pivotal moment in that career: its siting, spatial progression, and detail recall Wright, even as they reveal Lautner's own emerging voice,” reads the listing, adding that this is “an authentic piece of Los Angeles architectural history and a rare stewardship opportunity that may not come again.”

In addition to the striking interior design, another wow-worthy feature are views of the Hollywood Hills and San Gabriel Mountains.

What will also likely attract buyers is the location. As a haven for artists, it’s similar to the type of community that drew the Baldwins there back in the 1950s.

“Silver Lake has a very rich artist community and it’s vibrant, with young people, and there’s new cafes and a lot of nightlife happening in the area,” says Magnano. “There’s a lot of development happening in Silver Lake and a big restoration project taking place in the reservoir that the city of Los Angeles is getting ready to break ground on soon, to beautify the area.”

The ideal buyer, he says, is “somebody who understands the significance of these historical properties, who wants to restore them and honor them and keep them in the original glory that they all are. It was a family home for the Baldwins. They had three children. It could be a family home (again) but it could be somebody’s second home or ‘home away from home.’”

Based in Milwaukee, Kristine Hansen writes for TravelandLeisure.com, ArchitecturalDigest.com, Vogue.com, and other outlets. She’s also the author of “Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wisconsin: How America’s Most Famous Architect Found Inspiration in His Home State.” She lives in a 1924 bungalow.

#5680. STAT+: FDA, CMS scramble to avoid regulatory logjam as more states look to test AI in clinical settings

Mario covers technology in health care, including FDA regulation of artificial intelligence; how Medicare pays for health tech; the use of AI in clinical care; mental health chatbots; and consumer wearables. He’s also the co-author of the free, twice weekly STAT Health Tech newsletter. You can reach Mario on Signal at mariojoze.13.

Health officials hoping to boost adoption of artificial intelligence in health care have been moving behind the scenes to address brewing conflict between states and the federal government over the technology.

The Trump administration has sought to alleviate regulatory burden on companies developing health AI and created new ways to pay for the technology. But there remains a key problem: The federal government and states have overlapping jurisdiction over AI that performs clinical work, like writing prescriptions.

States regulate the practice of medicine and issue licenses to doctors and other clinicians. If AI performs these tasks without human supervision, that would likely push those products into the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration, which regulates medical devices.

#5679. Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues

Sutter Health calls off flagship hospital build in SF's East Bay, citing regulatory issues" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Sutter Health scrapped plans to build a flagship campus on property it owns in Emeryville, California, and instead is shifting its focus to outpatient care in the area, according to a Sept. 30 statement.

The health system announced those plans in early 2025 (see that story below), with a medical center of up to 200 beds as the centerpiece of a $1 billion investment into San Francisco's East Bay. It attributed its decision to "the lack of a clear and predictable regulatory path" related to California environmental and land use law.

"Over two years, we pursued relief under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA," the statement reads. "Those efforts did not secure the certainty needed to advance the hospital project, leaving it vulnerable to litigation that could delay construction and new hospital services for years."

Accompanying plans surrounding outpatient services "including primary and specialty care, diagnostic services and outpatient surgery" are now the priority for that community, though Sutter said it's still keeping an eye out for another potential location for a future hospital.

"Separating these projects keeps healthcare investment moving and allows us to advance additional outpatient services that can bring care to patients sooner. No alternative location has been selected, and we are assessing several options that can support comprehensive hospital, emergency and specialty care and the infrastructure needed for the future."

Sutter said that services will not be affected at Alta Bates, another hospital in the area it was planning to relieve with the new build, and that it plans to keep supporting that campus until another hospital can be finished. It added that hospitals across California have and continue to face "legal and regulatory challenges [tied to] significant seismic deadlines, while efforts to modernize or replace facilities can be exposed to lengthy regulatory reviews and litigation. A different location alone will not resolve these challenges."

Sutter Health will invest $1 billion to expand its services across Northern California's East Bay region, including a new flagship campus in Emeryville.

The health system announced Wednesday that the campus will feature a new medical center with up to 200 beds as well as a regional destination for ambulatory care. The plans also leave room for future expansion, according to the announcement.

The ambulatory services complex at the 12-acre campus will feature a wide array of specialties and will offer imaging and laboratory services. It expects to welcome its first patients as early as 2028, Sutter said.

The 335,000-square-foot medical center will include labor and delivery, surgical services, intensive care, emergency care and neonatal intensive care. The facility will be designed with the potential to add additional patient rooms in the future.

Sutter is targeting a 2032-33 opening date for the medical center, according to the announcement.

“Our Emeryville campus project represents one of the most significant investments we’re making across our system over the next decade and is part of our broader vision to meet the community’s growing demand for expanded access to our services across the East Bay footprint,” said Warner Thomas, president and CEO of Sutter Health, in the press release.

Sutter said it will put a focus on recruiting both primary care physicians and specialty care doctors, breaking down patient barriers to appointments and referrals and investing in initiatives to bolster the healthcare workforce. It expects to have 190 primary and specialty care clinicians staffing the new campus.

Beyond building the new campus, Sutter said it plans to grow the behavioral health services offered at its Herrick campus in Berkeley. The health system's Alta Bates campus will continue to operate as an acute care facility until the new medical center opens in Emeryville and then will be overhauled to provide ambulatory surgery services, urgent care and potentially skilled nursing services.

The health system is also renovating a medical office building in Berkley to serve as a primary care facility that will also offer OB-GYN care, according to the announcement.

Additional renovations are in the works as well, Sutter said.

“Too many people face challenges in accessing the care they need," Thomas said. "At Sutter, we’re committed to breaking down those barriers—expanding care facilities, enhancing imaging capabilities, improving online appointment scheduling and collaborating with the Sutter East Bay Medical Group and our community physician partners to attract more primary and specialty care physicians.

"These efforts will allow us to care for more patients while also investing in programs and partnerships that build the healthcare workforce of the future—ensuring more people get the right care when and where they need it," he said.

#5678. Opinion: What a mother’s 1834 letter about measles tells us about MAHA

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare.”

On Sept. 23, I sat in a small glass reading room at Yale’s medical library, turning the rag-paper pages of the Medical Dissenter, a London journal from the 1830s. At the bottom of one page, under the headline, “Report from Mrs. Butt to Mr. Hudson,” I met Jane Butt. Her letter was dated Sept. 23, 1834. I was reading it 192 years later to the day.

Jane lived in the village of Broughton and explained that measles had spread through the children around her earlier that year. She described how one of her own children had caught it. She then reported 36 other cases in her community. Some, she noted, developed severe inflammation of the lungs, one of the complications that can make measles deadly. She believed a cold east wind aggravated their symptoms. Nevertheless, she reported, all of them recovered.

Jane attributed the recoveries to Morison’s pills. James Morison was a merchant with no medical training who believed that a purgative could expel “impure blood” from the body and restore its natural balance. She administered the pills to the sick — sometimes twice a day — and gave as many as six at once to a toddler not yet 2 years old. She also gave the pills to women and, later, to their newborns, she wrote.

Morison’s followers called themselves Hygeists and attacked physicians as a monopoly that bled and poisoned its patients, which was not inaccurate in the 1830s. Much of medicine before the advent of germ theory and bacteriology provided incorrect diagnoses and problematic treatments.

When Jane wrote her letter, women could not train as physicians and were being displaced as midwives by the growing professional authority of doctors. She lacked medical credentials or the authority that came with them, but the Hygeist movement gave her a platform and a space to speak. She said that because “so much [was] said and done to prejudice the public mind against Mr. Morison’s most invaluable medicine,” she was left with no choice.

The journal that printed Jane’s letter sold the cure she praised. The office of the Medical Dissenter on the Strand was one of Morison’s official London depots for the pills in 1837. The same periodical mocked Edward Jenner, who had effectively used cowpox as a vaccination for smallpox, and ridiculed “vaccinic mania.”

After reading Jane’s story, I pulled out my iPhone and took photos of it, which I turned into a PDF. As a historian of medicine, I have seen cases of measles often in historical sources from the Civil War to life among the poor in tenement houses, but when I read those cases measles had long been the province of the past.

As I read Jane’s letter measles was back and raging in my home state of Pennsylvania, where six measles-associated deaths have been reported and federal health officials have disputed how many of them to count. In 2026, the United States has already recorded more than 4,500 measles cases, the largest number since 1991. Last school year, a record 4.2% of kindergartners were exempted from at least one required vaccine, and coverage for the measles vaccine fell to 92.4%, below the level needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. In some communities, the percentages of children who are vaccinated are far lower.

The current explosion of measles in the present had changed how I see the past. I didn’t preserve Jane’s story to indict her or to provide an antecedent to the unfounded arguments against vaccination, which have directly harmed innocent children. I documented her story instead because I had just finished a book on the ways ordinary people changed health care in the United States, and yet their stories have often been neglected, marginalized, or perceived to interfere with the real work of physicians. I wrote the book to show that medical knowledge is not an unalloyed concept created by professionals, but that ordinary people have continually provided evidence, offered interpretations, or even, in the case of Jane, simply counted the number of people who were sick in their communities.

Today, health populism takes shape in the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is rooted in part in grievances over how medical authority has dismissed patients, especially women. According to Politico, MAHA is “made up largely of women who followed Robert F. Kennedy Jr. into the MAGA fold.” Many of these women are moms. MAHA has, in turn, capitalized on the chauvinism of medical authority that began nearly 200 years ago that dismissed women as caregivers and often neglected their insights, their concerns, and their fears about epidemics.

The very act of counting, which might seem obvious or like a natural response to an epidemic, was part of a broader movement that eventually provided a framework for public health. Long before epidemiology developed as a discipline, patients and practitioners observed contagion — that disease seemed to spread from person to person, through households and across villages and nations. Before there was an official public health authority to count, people counted. Counting was also a move toward empiricism. It offered a bird’s-eye view of an epidemic and could provide local physicians or municipal authorities with some sense of the extent of an outbreak.

Counting mattered more than it might seem. Jane lived between two ways of explaining illness. In 1832, when a cholera pandemic reached New York City, clergy called for a national day of fasting and prayer. President Andrew Jackson refused to proclaim one, citing the separation of church and state, so states and churches held their own. Meanwhile, the city published daily counts of the sick and the dead. As the historian Charles Rosenberg showed in “The Cholera Years,” Americans read the epidemic as a judgment on sin even as they tracked it case by case. Jane blamed the wind and thanked God for her family’s recoveries, and she counted, reflecting the beginning of the shift from supernatural explanations to an empirical rationale. Documenting which children grew sickest and following an illness from house to house was a method aimed at articulating an explainable pattern. That method was not dissimilar to what physicians, ship surgeons, and military officials did in the first half of the 19th century when an epidemic erupted.

Jane’s method of dosing pills suffered from one problem: She did not observe what happened if a child did not receive the pills. Most children who caught measles in 1834 survived it, with or without pills. Thirty-seven recoveries indicated to her that the pills worked. They could not tell her what the pills did, or whether children like that toddler recovered despite them. Around the same time, the Paris physician Pierre Louis was also counting patients, and his numbers challenged bloodletting, one of medicine’s most trusted treatments, as a treatment for pneumonia. Louis asked what happened to comparable patients treated differently.

The vaccine does what Jane believed her pills did, and it was tested in ways her pills never were. Parents who refuse it are making Jane’s mistake in reverse.  She credited a cure that did nothing. They discount a protection that works, because measles has become a stranger.

Jane wrote her letter two years after the Provincial Medical and Surgical Association, a precursor to the British Medical Association, was founded in 1832 and more than a decade before the American Medical Association was founded in 1847 — a period in which men on both sides of the Atlantic were defining themselves as the institutional medical authority.

Ordinary people have been actively involved in the conversation since the beginning, but the medical populism of MAHA is making it appear as a new, novel, and even groundbreaking rebellion. Jane’s document reveals that ordinary people’s ideas have often been part of medicine, but medical authority has grown in ways that make them appear as dissenting.

Jane could not be heard in traditional medical circles. Sexism landed her in a fringe periodical, and her endorsement of the quackery of purgatives gave her a headline.

If men had not systematically excluded women from medicine and had recognized that ordinary people’s ideas, insights, and concerns are part of it, Jane might not have reached for purgative pills, and women today might not be reaching for pyrotechnic platforms to be heard.

I have been trained not to write in the conditional tense but instead to explain what happened and how it all went down. I wasn’t looking for her. I found her by accident, but I am drawn to ordinary people’s stories. That’s why I found Jane’s letter so appealing. Before I contextualized it and realized it was part of a radical publication, I was amazed to see the name of a woman in a headline in boldface in a rare book.

Although Jane does not appear in my book, she embodies its thesis — even though her method was wrong. In fact, much of medical practice was wrong or ineffective before the late 19th century, and plenty remained so afterward. There were many ordinary people, like Jane, who witnessed outbreaks and illness in their communities and reported what they saw.

When I closed the volume containing Jane’s letter and walked out of the secure room, through the Victorian reading room, through the rotunda, and past the portraits of physicians whose names circle its walls, Jane’s name was not there, nor were those of any other women from 200 years ago.

It does not have to continue to be that way. Ordinary people’s voices matter and they often begin not in the throes of a national polemic or screamed through a speaker at a MAHA rally but begin, like Jane, with an observation of a child’s health.

Jim Downs is the author of “Medicine by the People: How Ordinary People Changed American Healthcare” (W. W. Norton, October 2026). He is the Gilder Lehrman–NEH professor of history at Gettysburg College and a visiting faculty fellow at Brown University’s Center for the Study of Race and Ethnicity in America. He is a 2025–26 Guggenheim fellow.

#5677. Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds

Weekly Rundown: Doximity launches DoseCheck; AI recommends costlier care than doctors, study finds" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Oct. 26 to 30.

Doximity launched DoseCheck, a new safety feature within Doximity Ask designed to catch unsafe or incorrect medication dosing recommendations generated by artificial intelligence.

Doximity Ask is the company's clinical decision support tool.

Rather than relying on an LLM to double-check another LLM, DoseCheck adds a deterministic, rule-based verification layer, checking AI-generated dosing claims against structured information including FDA labeling and professional guidelines, the company said. By checking against FDA labeling and professional guidelines, DoseCheck increases accuracy to more than 99%, the company claims.

Doximity tested nine widely used AI models with over 8,000 dosing questions based on real physician queries. At least 2.3% of dosing claims made by these models were wrong, and 43.8% of detected errors were serious or potentially lethal.

According to the analysis, common sources of errors include dosing newer drugs, failing to account for patient-specific factors such as kidney function, age, weight and medical history, and mistakes involving units, decimal points or drugs with similar names.

"AI is probabilistic. Drug dosing can’t be," said Louis-Antoine Mullie, M.D., chief AI researcher at Doximity. "DoseCheck doesn’t ask a language model to grade its own homework. It checks dosing claims against a structured, authoritative database, so physicians get the same verified dosing answer every time."

DoseCheck is free and has been rolled out to all Doximity Ask users across mobile and desktop.

Health and wellness platform Hims & Hers plans to launch a peptides specialty after the federal government signaled it will allow compounding pharmacies to manufacture six peptides temporarily.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services will not take action against licensed pharmacists who dispense certain unapproved peptides, according to a new policy published this week in the Federal Register.

Stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued Wednesday, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

The specific compounds included (PDF) in the list are BPC-157, epitalon, KPV, MOTS-c, semax and TB-500, all of which were discussed in a meeting of the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) in July, with the panel ultimately voting to recommend including the treatments onto the 503A Bulk Drug Substances list.

Through its new Peptides+ specialty, Hims & Hers plans to offer access to Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable. "If a customer is eligible, a personalized treatment plan will be prescribed and delivered by independent providers, treatments supplied by licensed pharmacies, with ongoing clinical support our customers can trust," CEO Andrew Dudum wrote in a blog post.

"We’re focused on entering this specialty the right way, not the fastest. Most of what we know about these compounds is still early—with limited published studies, we draw primarily from clinical experience from the last decade. We’ve consistently acknowledged that while these compounds hold promise, there is still information we do not yet know. Provider-supervised use is how we plan to build on this foundation and make sure that access and innovation can move at the same pace," Dudum said.

The tech giant launched Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate, a new program designed to teach healthcare professionals responsible, practical ways to use AI in their day-to-day work. Clinicians at Google developed the virtual course, and the program is accredited for up to five American Medical Association (AMA) continuing education credits.

The NYU Grossman School of Medicine, the University of Alabama at Birmingham and Touro University are offering the program to their faculty, residents and medical students. Leading nursing institutions, including Purdue University School of Nursing, are offering the certificate as part of their healthcare professional training, according to Google.

"As I’ve traveled around the world this year, I’ve heard loud and clear from healthcare professionals how much need there is for a thoughtful but practical educational resource on AI, made specifically for healthcare," Michael Howell, M.D., Google’s chief health officer, wrote in a blog post.

Large language models recommend more up-front testing, referrals and treatment than the physicians who actually saw the patients and at more than three times the cost, according to a study published in NEJM AI.

Researchers from the Technion, Stanford University and collaborating institutions tested 20 general-purpose and four specialized medical AI systems on records from 200 real outpatient and emergency visits. Each received the clinical presentation without the physician’s assessment and plan. The team priced the recommended tests and referrals in both the AI and physicians’ plans using the same 2026 Medicare rates.

Across the 20 general-purpose systems, AI-suggested care cost a mean of $314 per visit, compared with $97 for care recommended by attending physicians. Suggested care was more costly in 180 of 200 cases. The average cost of care per AI system ranged from $209 to $599.

Diagnostic testing rose from $71 per visit in the physicians’ plans to $176 across the systems, about $105 more per visit. The referral rates for the physician’s plans were 0.15 per visit compared to 0.87 for the LLM’s plans, which, at the corresponding Medicare rates, is $111 more per visit, according to the study.

"The four specialized medical systems showed comparable excess (2.7× to 3.5×), so medical fine-tuning did not curb—and may reinforce—cost escalation," the study authors wrote.

The researchers used MTSamples, a publicly available collection of 4,999 real de-identified medical transcription sample reports contributed by practicing clinicians as reference material for medical transcriptionists. The notes are documentation from real patient visits, but they are a convenience sample assembled for transcription training rather than a representative draw from U.S. ambulatory practice, the study authors wrote.

"Under a single standard prompt, every AI system we evaluated, general purpose and medically specialized alike, suggested more diagnostic tests, medications and specialist referrals than the treating physician on the same cases," the study authors wrote.

LLMs appear optimized to be comprehensive and avoid missing diagnoses, and may show an analogous tendency toward exhaustive workup, the study authors noted.

The researchers argued that much of the excess can be reduced through better prompting, suggesting cost inflation is partly a deployment and design problem rather than an unavoidable feature of AI.

Researchers reevaluated 19 models using different instructions. A simple cost-aware prompt telling models to recommend only clinically necessary, cost-effective items reduced average recommended costs from 3.2 times physician costs to 2.5 times.

A stronger "parsimonious-but-safe" prompt told models to focus on the three most likely diagnoses, explicitly rule out dangerous "cannot-miss" conditions, and recommend only tests whose results would change management. That cut costs to just 1.4 times physician costs. But diagnostic agreement with physicians fell in 17 of the 19 systems, illustrating why cost reductions need to be evaluated alongside other changes in the recommendations, the study authors noted.

"Getting the diagnosis right matters, but so does the path you take to get there," said Prof. Dvir Aran of the Technion, the study’s corresponding author, in a statement. "Accuracy and safety have dominated how clinical AI is trained and evaluated. Efficiency needs the same attention: whether each test or referral is likely to help the patient."

Digital health company Eko Health launched a new stethoscope, the CORE 300, that integrates traditional and digital listening modes directly into a single chestpiece.

The AI-enabled stethoscope, which received FDA clearance, is also in line with premium traditional stethoscopes, making the digital technology more accessible to a broader group of healthcare professionals, the company said.

With a twist of the chestpiece, clinicians can switch between familiar traditional listening and Eko’s advanced digital listening technology, with up to 35x amplification, active noise cancellation and real-time heart rate displayed directly on the device. When connected to the Eko App and Eko's FDA-cleared AI for structural murmur detection, CORE 300 can also bring AI disease detection into the physical exam.

"Millions of healthcare professionals around the world use a stethoscope to examine patients every day," said Connor Landgraf, co-founder and CEO of Eko Health, in a statement. "Our goal is to bring the most ubiquitous clinical exam into the precise digital era. Once the physical exam becomes digital, we combine better listening with objective measurements and AI-powered clinical decision support right at the point of care."Clinical technologies are evolving quickly, but adoption depends on making new capabilities fit naturally into the way clinicians already practice, said Steven R. Steinhubl, M.D., chief medical officer of Eko Health and a board-certified cardiologist.

"CORE 300 bridges that gap. It preserves the traditional experience of auscultation while putting enhanced digital listening, objective measurements, and access to clinical decision support a twist of the chestpiece away. That combination can help make a smarter, more connected physical exam a routine part of care rather than the exception," Steinhubl said.

With Eko's digital stethoscope, clinicians can record, visualize and save heart, lung and body sounds and interpret the data with Eko’s FDA-cleared AI and software. According to the company, the device could expand screening capabilities in primary care offices, busy clinics and rural healthcare settings.

Eko Health launched its first Eko CORE digital stethoscope attachment in 2025, and to date, has delivered more than 750,000 digital stethoscopes and AI-enabled devices worldwide.

Healthcare engagement and payment solutions provider RevSpring debuted a conversational intelligent virtual agent that helps patients manage payment plans over the phone.

Let’s Talk expands on RevSpring’s voice platform and is integrated with its payment portal. It gives patients the ability to make payments, create payment plans, ask questions and respond to outbound voice reminders.

Initial results of the tool show a 36% increase in patient payment rates and a 27% decrease in transfer to live agents, the company says. Moreover, average call durations decreased 25% with Let’s Talk.

“Healthcare organizations are looking for ways to automate more patient interactions and improve financial outcomes without losing sight of the need for patient empathy,” said Scott MacKenzie, RevSpring CEO, in a statement. “Adding payment plans to Let’s Talk expands what patients can accomplish through conversational self-service, helping more callers resolve their needs without transferring to a representative. We’re building on years of proven payment automation to help providers improve efficiency and scale self-service across the patient financial experience.”

Enterprise healthcare operations software provider symplr launched Monday an integrated workforce management solution combining AI-driven scheduling and timekeeping.

The tool—dubbed symplr Time and Scheduling—combines symplr’s predictive nurse and staffing scheduling tool with its timekeeping solution. Nurse managers can identify and address staffing gaps "hundreds of days in advance," ultimately reducing time spent on staffing and timecard tasks by approximately 50%, executives say.

"Nurse leaders shouldn’t have to spend hours building schedules and scrambling to fill open shifts when they could be supporting their teams and patients," said Ali Morin, symplr chief nursing informatics officer, in a statement. "Nurses want more flexibility and predictability, while health systems need the right people in the right place at the right time. We designed symplr Time and Scheduling to deliver both, giving nurses and nurse leaders more time for patient care and less time managing the work around it."

Additional AI capabilities are expected to roll out in 2027, the company says.

Cleveland Clinic Cancer Institute launched an AI task force Monday in a bid to evaluate the technologies and streamline adoption in a "safe and deliberate manner."

The task force is dubbed the Cancer Institute Office of Technology and Digital Strategy. It is led by Paul Thambi, M.D., and Louis Williams, M.D. AI is currently being used by the institute to personalize radiation doses, reduce note-taking time and streamline patient referral processes, according to the Oct. 27 announcement.

Williams said in a statement that it’s "crucial to have a system to continuously re-evaluate the effectiveness of each tool," adding that outputs of models should be analyzed on "an ongoing basis."

"There can be drift in a model that may influence its accuracy over time or there may be bias in the model that isn’t apparent upfront," Williams said. "That’s why it’s necessary to have a unified strategy that includes training models to identify mistakes before a model goes into production as well as longitudinal risk assessment to ensure safety."

#5676. The persisting paradox of men’s health

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Annalisa (Nalis) Merelli is focused on boys’ and men’s health: She looks into reproductive health, trending treatments, screening approaches, mental health, and everything in between.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.

Buongiorno! As you put the final touches on your Halloween costumes, here is a spooky story for you: Imagine going to urgent care for something as trivial as a UTI, and getting a bill for $1,756, on top of $211 you already paid at the clinic! Keep reading to learn more.

Intuitive Health, a private equity-backed company that runs about 50 hybrid ER-urgent care clinics, was launched on the idea that it could offer an alternative to costly hospital visits, providing under the same roof a clinic for uncomplicated issues and an ER in case of necessity.

But for many patients, the opposite has happened: They came in with simple, urgent care-appropriate conditions but were billed for ER services — think close to $2,000 for an UTI or $7,000 ($2,100 after insurance) for congestion and cough. Company officials say every patient should be asked to sign a form before the “upgrade,” but Tara Bannow found in her investigation this was far from standard practice.

A federal judge in Massachusetts has rejected the federal government’s definition of “medical frailty,” ruling that states didn’t have enough time to assess eligibility status. The decision overturns an interim CMS rule that substantially limited the pool of people eligible for exemptions to the work requirements, in particular by requiring that medically frail people demonstrate that their condition prevents them from working. The rule also didn’t list conditions that would automatically be exempt from work requirements.

The lawsuit was brought on by states claiming that CMS didn’t have the authority to narrow the definition of medically frail, and that the rule would create red tape for beneficiaries having to demonstrate their status, as well as an additional burden for state workers. Thursday’s ruling complicates the already tangled web of work requirements, and might lead to a delay in their rollout past the beginning of 2027, when they were slated to go into effect. More here.

At a rally for Zach Lahn, the farmer-turned-unlikely Republican candidate for Iowa governor, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. called Lahn’s opposition to Big Agriculture, a key tenet of his platform, a “spiritual battle.”

“We have to figure out a way to grow food without poisoning our kids, without giving ourselves cancer, without destroying the soils that enrich us and enrich our microbiome that connect our brain and all of our organs. And make us healthy, robust and vibrant people,” Kennedy told the crowd.

Chelsea Cirruzzo, who reported on the rally, also takes a broader look at RFK Jr.’s big talking points, with the midterms around the corner: fighting fraud, doubling down on “medical freedom” in the form of vaccine choice, and pushing MAHA, even as the political future of the movement looks shaky. (Also don’t forget to check out our 2026 midterms roundup for the most important political news.)

People who are diagnosed with colorectal cancer earlier in life, especially younger than 35, often have a grimmer prognosis than people who develop the disease older. Researchers have been trying to understand why. A new “atlas” of 189 colorectal cancer tumors from patients in their 20s to their 90s could help explain the differences in the disease, while controlling for variables that may have confounded previous studies.

“It is devastating to care for young patients diagnosed with often advanced stages of colorectal cancer. These are people in the prime of their life,” Kimmie Ng, the colorectal cancer researcher who authored the database study, told Angus Chen. “That’s what motivates us to do the work, find out what might be causing this, and what unique features we could target so that we can better treat these patients. It’s something that keeps me up at night, and one of the biggest questions facing our scientific community today.”

Ng, who serves as the director of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, discussed in a Q&A what kinds of insights the database might offer, and what her team is learning about the increasing rate of colorectal cancer in young patients.

A new series in The Lancet argues for the need to investigate a paradox of men’s health: why men experience worse health outcomes than women, even though they hold undeniable privilege. In their approach, the series authors move away from looking at men’s health as an issue of sex, broadening the frame to focus on gender. “Men’s health is defined and shaped by the culturally defined roles, responsibilities, attributes, and entitlements associated with being (or being seen as) a man, as well as power relations between and among women and men,” they write in the introduction.

A first paper proposes a framework that analyzes men’s health through an intersectional lens, focusing on structural determinants of health. A second looks at the available data about men’s life expectancy and burden of disability, trying — with limitations due to the lack of an intersectional perspective in many of the studies so far — to tease out risk factors and causes. The third paper proposes a political strategy that advances men’s health as a contributing factor to the shared public good.

Discussion of men’s health is wont to raise the question of whether it is detracting from women’s. The authors defend their choice. “A gendered approach to health is not a zero-sum game; it can serve to enhance wellbeing for all,” they write.

This week, STAT Executive Editor Rick Berke travelled to Washington, D.C., to accept in memory of Helen Branswell the Kovler Prize for Trust in Life Science Journalism at the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health dinner. It was an elegant event at Union Station, with 350 luminaries from science and health, including current and former NIH directors.

The highlight of the evening was a video that Helen recorded in late summer to accept the award. She talked about her work and a career she so deeply loved. As readers of this newsletter know, Helen has been a frequent contributor to Morning Rounds over the last 11 years, tirelessly sharing her insights on infectious disease news. (In fact, Helen’s first writings on Covid-19 appeared here.)

Heartbroken as we all are by her loss, I hope you’ll watch and come away inspired but one of the truly greats.

#5674. Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans

Why Oscar Health is putting a focus on personalization for ACA exchange plans" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Another open enrollment period is set to begin on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges, and the team at Oscar Health is focusing on the unique ways it can innovate in the turbulent market.

Oscar is growing the number of counties in its geographic footprint by 24% in 2027, offering plans across 713 counties in 21 states. It is also investing in new specialized plans, such as its RetireEase offering, and in expanding coverage options designed for individuals with certain conditions.

Janet Liang, president of Oscar Insurance, told Fierce Healthcare that it's critical for plans to learn as much as they can about the individual consumer, so that they can shape benefits that effectively meet the needs of the people who are coming to the marketplaces for coverage.

"We are completely dialed in to the individual consumer," she said. "We know the people who are in the ACA, and it's a broad, broad range of people. It's not one size fits all, and what we do is we spend the time to understand who comes into the ACA and what are the services and needs that individuals have."

That includes putting a focus on collecting plenty of feedback from existing members, and what they're searching for as existing enrollees, as well as collecting data on broader consumer behaviors on the exchanges.

The RetireEase plan, for example, was born from this thinking, Liang said. The offering, which is launching in five states next year, aims to support members in the transition to Medicare coverage, targeted to people aged 55 to 64.

Benefits include set prices for key services in this age range, from preventive care to physical therapy to cardiology. Members that enroll in RetireEase can also access specific supports designed for the handoff to Medicare, for caregivers and transportation if needed.

Liang said this population tends to have unique concerns about affordability as employers shift their approaches in a way that is leading more people to retire early, leaving them on a fixed income. It's also an age range where people begin to develop challenging chronic conditions that will need to be managed in the future.

The team took that feedback and those particular needs it heart when building out RetireEase, Liang said.

Oscar's suite of specialized offerings includes some of its most popular plans, she said. In addition to the new launch, Oscar is expanding the reach of its existing specialized plans. HelloMeno, its plan designed for women navigating menopause, will grow to 15 states by 2027, for example.

Liang said that these plans have higher Net Promoter Scores than its traditional plans, and they also tend to have higher retention rates than the broader offerings.

"Based on the retention rate and the high NPS scores, we know that we're meeting an unmet need," she said.

And the Oscar team is already planning for the future around these specialized plans, and has determined where to go next for 2028. Expanding this slate is a central part of Oscar's broader strategy around the ACA, which also includes enhancements to bronze, silver and gold plans as well as a focus on individual coverage health reimbursement arrangements, or ICHRA.

ICHRA plans have rebranded as Custom Health Option and Individual Care Expense, or CHOICE. But in these models, an employer offers workers a stipend to purchase an exchange plan, rather than offering coverage directly.

Liang said Oscar believes this is an area that will continue to grow. She said that they're seeing higher numbers of employers requesting quotes for potential CHOICE arrangements, and Oscar has doubled its membership between 2025 and 2026.

She added that Oscar expects to triple its CHOICE market share by 2029.

"So there's an obvious interest by employers to reduce their costs," Liang said. "And we also look at markets where there's just a lot of interest by both small employers, regional employers, to just start off. What you see is new employers and new companies that are forming will go straight to CHOICE instead of starting on the traditional insurance path."
