#5536. As Anthropic finally files for its IPO, rising risks aren’t slowing the AI buildout – yet

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

The other artificial intelligence shoe dropped this week, as Anthropic filed for what surely will be the second blockbuster AI initial public offering of stock this year.

Nearly 70,000 words in the filing list a ton of risks, but in short, it’s making unimaginably huge bets on buying computing power, it’s uncertain on how long customers will keep spending on AI in the face of dubious returns — and of course there’s the really-not-unusual “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” And as Jason Bloomberg writes, the unmentioned risk is that AI as of today doesn’t have the economies of scale that made software so lucrative.

But it’s hard to imagine it won’t be crazily successful if and when it happens before Thanksgiving. They’ll join the 70% of Nvidia employees who are millionaires. Shed another tear for anyone looking for affordable housing in the Bay Area — we’re not building our way out of this, no matter what YIMBY folks hope.

One interesting wrinkle: SpaceXAI, the other AI IPO earlier this year, will be hoping Anthropic’s offering is successful, since it’s supplying a large chunk of that compute. Same with other AI partner/rivals such as Google and Microsoft.

And Anthropic isn’t alone in amassing cash to continue buying and building more AI infrastructure. Meta this week said it will issue $95 billion in nonvoting stock to build even more. Few, least of all universal backstop Nvidia, seem to think the AI and data center backlash will dent this investment. But that doesn’t mean everyone will win. As SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said this week, self-servingly but perhaps not wrongly (Gartner agrees), a lot of AI neoclouds are going to go belly-up.

Investor worry extends to the big cloud providers too. Despite a continued boom in its cloud business, Google parent Alphabet saw its stock swoon more than 12% Thursday, vaporizing more than $500 billion in market value as it reported a slow quarter for search and ads — perhaps because AI chatbots are siphoning off people’s attention. Microsoft fared better thanks to its resilient application layer on which it can apply AI. But despite strong cloud revenue growth, Amazon stock fell on concerns it could be spending too much on infrastructure. All that came to a head Friday, when the Nasdaq tanked, down almost 3%.

Seems like investors are just generally skittish. On a tear this year until now, Intel stock plunged almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report, on concerns the PC business is slowing. Fortinet also fell more than 20% following its report that included a slightly lower outlook.

For some wider perspective on the AI buildout and what’s needed to make it pay off, check out Dave Vellante’s Breaking Analysis, a late addition here Saturday, a conversation with analyst Crawford Del Prete.

Don’t relax yet. Next week there’s another earningspalooza, including Apple, AMD, Supermicro, Qualcomm, Arm and Palantir.

So an apparent Chinese spy for some time has been hanging around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who evidently didn’t know she was more than a customer executive. Lordy. The New York Times laid out the bones of the U.S. government’s concern, but read it carefully and it sure seems like there are some missing dots throughout. Perhaps this kind of espionage is more common than we know where there’s a nexus of big money and geopolitics, but this may not be the last we hear of it, even if the Trump administration is shrugging.

Oh, and there’s an election next week that might change things… in unpredictable, not necessarily great ways for the economy. Fasten those seatbelts. And vote (but not for the wrong people, thanks).

#5535. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5534. Krafton-backed Ludo Robotics releases robot intelligence model designed around human intent

Ludo Robotics Inc., a subsidiary of major South Korean video game publisher Krafton Inc., today debuted Ludi 0.2, a robotics artificial intelligence system built to understand people and interact with them in the physical world.

Headquartered in Palo Alto, Ludo spun out of Krafton, a company that primarily publishes video games and is best known for the ultra-popular “PUBG: Battlegrounds.” Ludo also has a research and development lab in Seoul where it combines the efforts of researchers and engineers across robotics, machine learning and AI.

Krafton Chief Executive CH Kim also helms Ludo as CEO, with Krafton’s Chief AI Officer Kangwook Lee serving as its chief technology officer.

Why did a video game company form and back an AI robotics company? Krafton said it believes AI makes games more responsive and replayable. It also has strong roots in simulation, interaction and real-time systems, which have immediate applications in the bridge between the digital and physical, where the interaction between humans and robots lives.

“Robots are becoming increasingly capable of performing physical tasks, but understanding and responding to people remains a major challenge,” said Lee. “Ludi 0.2 represents another step toward our goal of bringing conversation, reasoning and physical action together so robots can better understand human intent, respond to feedback and adapt as situations change.”

The company introduced the first version of Ludi 0.1 in August 2026. It combines a vision-language model for reasoning and dialogue with specialized navigation and manipulation capabilities. Today’s next-generation model has advanced its capabilities, forming more natural human-robot interaction, including social intelligence, memory and reasoning, tool coordination, gesture interpretation, and physical movement.

The company said it’s working toward a final version of Ludi that will integrate perception, dialogue and physical action.

The objective is to integrate communication, reasoning and physical action into one “brain.” The model would watch what’s happening, listen to commands and speech, interpret those commands alongside human gestures and physical movements and reason about the environment. This would happen in real time, coordinating similarly to how another human decides on actions based on another person’s actions in their workspace.

This is the “Holy Grail” of physical AI, where intelligent robots can perform actions not just in industrial environments and warehouses, but also retail and domestic spaces such as restaurants, living rooms and kitchens.

Krafton said much of its work includes proprietary foundation models and co-playable characters developed in collaboration with Nvidia Corp., AI teammates designed to understand players in real time. Ludo builds on this foundation to develop the same kind of intelligence into real-world robots.

Startups are bringing the physical world to robots so they can see objects and grab and move them with increasing capability. Interpreting human intent and responding to social cues from people around the robot, however, remains elusive. Simulation makes it easy for physical AI to prepare robots to work with objects and around humans, but it doesn’t always prepare them to model human behavior.

#5533. Nicholas Cage Says He’s a ‘Bit Homeless’ and ‘Living in Hotels’ After Sinkhole Damaged $10.5 Million Malibu Home

Actor Nicolas Cage has been displaced after coastal erosion caused a growing sinkhole in the driveway of his Malibu, CA, home.

"I'm currently a little bit homeless," the "National Treasure" star, 62, said at an Oct. 31 appearance at L.A. Comic Con. "Something happened to my house in Malibu, so I'm just sort of living in hotels so I don't have normal trick-or-treaters I would like to enjoy tonight."

Cage was still in the spooky holiday spirit, noting that he had planned to take his daughter, August, 4, trick-or-treating in Santa Monica later that night.

The devastation comes just two years after Cage snapped up his 4,000-square-foot beachfront home for $10.5 million.

The 30-square-foot sinkhole that first appeared on Cage's property collapsed on Sept. 6, leaving a 900-square-foot sinkhole in its place.

Jonathan Torres, a public information officer with the LACFD, said the collapse likely resulted from coastal erosion. Witnesses at the scene said they could see waves crashing through the hole. Cage was reportedly not at home at the time of the incident.

Cage is not the only famous resident of Sea Level Drive, the exclusive gated community where the disaster took place. Pierce Brosnan, Dustin Hoffman, and Mindy Kaling live in the neighborhood, as well.

Initially, a state of emergency was declared, and the city of Malibu red-tagged seven nearby homes, prohibiting homeowners from accessing the properties. It later red-tagged 24 additional properties in the community, noting that "current road erosion prevents normal ingress and egress to the neighborhood, and would also prevent access or evacuation routes in the event of an emergency."

At the time of the incident, the neighborhood's homeowners association had already begun repairs, which it estimates could take up to five weeks to complete.The ocean-facing abode, which comes with a secluded beach and a rare roof deck, first came on the market in March 2024 for $11.25 million, according to Realtor.com®. The waterfront residence had also been simultaneously offered for rent for $25,000 a month.

The property comes with a private courtyard and a two-car garage, which is equipped with an elevator. The living room, bathed in natural light, has a vaulted ceiling, a chic bar area, and a fireplace.

Floor-to-ceiling glass walls and sliding doors seamlessly connect the indoor and outdoor spaces.

On the second level is a chef's kitchen with high-end stainless appliances, a center island, and sweeping ocean views.

The third floor features four en suite bedrooms, along with a primary bedroom facing the Pacific Ocean, with a spa-worthy bath, fireplace, and ocean-facing deck.

In addition to the home's beach frontage, the property includes an adjacent beach lot.

Prior to that purchase, Cage faced troubles with an infamous "haunted" mansion in New Orleans' French Quarter.

In 2009, the actor lost the property to foreclosure, and it was subsequently purchased by Regions Bank for $4.5 million.

The following year, the home was sold to an investor for $2.1 million.

Before that March 2024 listing, the property had bounced on and off the market since summer 2022 and had once been offered for as much as $17.9 million.

By comparison, Cage seems to have secured an impressive deal—although, judging by the success of his onscreen endeavor that year, paying the full ask might not have been out of the question for him.

In 2024, the actor and producer appeared in the horror film "Longlegs," which became the "highest grossing independent film of the year," with $100 million at the box office, according to Variety.

The "Face/Off" star is also known to keep a full-time residence in Nevada, the site of his iconic movies "Leaving Las Vegas" and "Honeymoon in Vegas."

Cage has a lengthy real estate history in California.

In fact, he owned a San Francisco Queen Anne Victorian, which he picked up in 1989 and held for 16 years. He sold the property some 20 years ago, but left behind personal touches, including custom stained-glass windows.

Although Cage has seemingly been left without a home in Malibu, he does have property on the East Coast. In March 2026, he reportedly snapped up a sprawling two-bedroom condo in the heart of Manhattan for $6.5 million—and took out a $4.55 million mortgage for the deal.The actor is said to have purchased the unit in the Essex House Residences building at 160 Central Park South for a steep $1.4 million discount—after the property initially hit the market for $7.9 million.

The home measures 2,400 square feet and is a combination of two units, as first reported by The Real Deal.

The listing described it as offering "an unparalleled blend of elegance, comfort, and convenience, right at the doorstep of Central Park."

Cage will likely feel right at home inside Essex House, which has played host to many famous faces over the years, including the late actor and musician David Bowie and his wife, Iman.

Oasis star Liam Gallagher also purchased a pad in the unit in 2012, selling it two years later.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5532. Extreme Networks wants the network to run AI, not just be run by it

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

At its recent AI Summit in Amsterdam, Extreme Networks Inc. shared early Agent ONE Coworker results and previewed Exchange zones, which put spare access points and switch compute to work as on-premises artificial intelligence infrastructure. Here’s what it means and what information technology pros should do about it.

Most of the conversation about AI and networking has flowed in one direction. AI comes in, examines the network and helps the network team run it better. That’s useful, but it treats the network as the patient, not as a resource.

At the summit, the company argued that there is a better way. The network should be managed by AI and serve as a place where AI runs, using data that most organizations currently throw away. This would let network teams stop being the people who merely keep the Wi-Fi up for the AI project and become the people who host it.

Extreme made two announcements. The first was a progress report on Extreme Agent ONE Coworker, the ambient AI agent built into Extreme Platform ONE. In its first month, Extreme says, customers saved about 1,000 hours of troubleshooting, 41% of Platform ONE customers used it for daily tasks, and users responded to 98% of critical “nudges,” the proactive alerts the agent raises after running its own pre-investigation. Engagement was roughly 10 times that of Extreme’s first-generation conversational assistant.

The second was a preview of Extreme Exchange zones, planned for the first half of 2027. A zone combines an Extreme Universal Compute Platform or a customer-owned server with spare capacity from Extreme access points and switches already installed at a site. AI applications from the Extreme Exchange marketplace run locally on open-weight models by default, with cloud inference used only when policy allows and logged every time. Agent ONE Operator mode, the autonomous tier, also arrives in the first half of 2027.

The first wave of AI in networking wasn’t a smashing success because it relied on a chatbot built on fragmented data. During his talk, Nabil Bukhari (pictured), Extreme’s chief technology officer and president of AI platforms, called it a design flaw. “Conversational AI requires the user to have the question and the context, and you will be surprised how difficult that is when it comes to technology domains,” he said.

In Extreme’s focus groups, many administrators asked a powerful AI assistant how many devices they had, even though the number was already on the dashboard. Coworker flips that. “We have moved to the world where instead of you prompting AI, AI prompts you,” Bukhari said.

The best evidence came from a customer. Kevin Rocha, chief information officer at Hill College, described a wireless outage in a building housing HR, finance and enrollment. “Agent ONE Coworker told me exactly where to look: One access point needed attention, and several more were due for firmware upgrades. We resolved the issue in about 20 minutes rather than an entire morning,” he said. Platform ONE, he added, “is like having two or three more network engineers on staff.”

That’s the value of AI for networking in most enterprises. It doesn’t replace the network team. It gives a small team the reach of a larger one. Bukhari also admitted that there is more work to be done. He explained that 58% of support cases opened by Agent ONE arrive with all the evidence support needs. “Fifty-eight is pretty good, but 58 is still 58 and not 100.”

Andrew Grill, the opening keynote speaker and author of “Digitally Curious,” discussed the stakes. “When a chatbot gets it wrong, you might have a bad paragraph. If an agent gets it wrong, you have a bad Tuesday,” he said. His test for any deployment: “If your agent does something wrong at 2 in the morning, whose phone rings?”

Extreme’s Operator demo is subject to guardrails. Each of the 268 tools can be configured to auto-authorize, ask first or never use. Four baseline rules apply to everything: do no harm to the network, never expose a credential, never act outside your role and never act in another tenant. Every task has a full audit trace.

An important design criterion is that governance reside within Extreme Exchange, not Platform ONE. “You can’t govern something from within,” Bukhari said. “That is how you get rogue agents.” If the system running the agent also controls its permissions, you don’t have a control plane. You have an honor system.

Networks generate dense, real-time telemetry on location, movement and behavior that far exceeds what operations needs, and cloud platforms drop most of it because moving it is expensive. Bukhari said the valuable uses tend to hit four walls: sovereignty, localization, survivability and economics.

The innovation is where the compute comes from. Higher-end access points have four to eight cores and typically use only one, so organizations already pay for and power idle compute hanging from their ceilings. In one healthcare demo, a fall-detection app that combined camera feeds, Wi-Fi location and paging to find the closest responder ran entirely on access points. A second demo used Seattle Seahawks game data to predict gate congestion and showed that some fans faced a seven- to eight-minute walk to the nearest pro shop.

“This is not a network management use case,” Bukhari said. “These use cases are impossible without that rich, real-time telemetry.” That’s the strategic point. The return goes to operations, facilities and fan experience, giving network leaders something they’ve rarely had: a revenue story.

Zones will ship in 2027, and the demo apps were built in collaboration with design partners. The model needs a real application catalog, so Extreme is pairing it with a free, invitation-only forward-deployed engineering program. Pricing will be consumption-based, measured in “agent actions.” As Grill noted, most organizations haven’t priced the cost of their tasks today, so they’ll struggle to judge value.

As expected, the most valuable insights came from the customer panel. Jonathan Monk, CIO of the Institute of Cancer Research in London, manages roughly 9 petabytes of data, but performance isn’t his primary reason for building sovereign AI. “When we ask people in our organization what’s the biggest thing that holds them back from using AI, it’s that I’m not sure if I’m allowed to,” he said.

Andrew Beynon, chief enterprise architect at Extreme partner ARO, linked that to shadow AI. The goal, he said, is “to make the journey for legitimate adoption of AI easier than the move to illegitimate adoption.” Monk called it building “paved roads.” The industry treats sovereignty as a compliance cost, but these customers see it as an adoption accelerator.

David O’Neill, director of IT operations at Liverpool Football Club, offered a balanced take on AI. “While AI is an answer, it’s not necessarily the answer.” Bukhari highlighted the next challenge: “Adoption is no longer the problem. It’s the optimization of adoption.” After AI-generated product specs ballooned to 200 pages, Extreme capped them at three pages.

Include the network team in the AI plan. If it isn’t involved, decisions about traffic, inference location and data residency will be made without the people who understand them.

Separate governance from execution. Check whether agent permissions, audit logs and the kill switch are outside the system the agent runs in.

Inventory the data your network discards. Identify the location and occupancy telemetry you already generate, and which business units would pay to use them.

Pressure-test the edge-compute math. Ask how workloads are prioritized during RF demand spikes and which model sizes realistically fit on an access point.

Price your tasks first. Without a baseline cost for today’s work, it’s impossible to evaluate consumption-based AI pricing.

Extreme can’t outspend its larger competitors, so it’s betting on speed and focus as a pure-play networking company. The Agent ONE numbers suggest that’s paying off on the operations side.

Exchange zones are the bolder idea. Turning installed access points and switches into a distributed, centrally governed inference fabric is more ambitious than anything I’ve seen from Extreme’s larger rivals. It’s also unproven, and 2027 is a long way off in AI time. As Beynon put it, “today’s knowledge has got an expiry date.”

The direction Extreme is headed is the right one. For 30 years, the network has been the most important infrastructure, yet nobody wanted to talk about it until it broke. AI makes the network the system that connects data, compute and people, and possibly the one that runs the AI, too. Network pros who see that early will have a much bigger role in where their organizations go next.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5531. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5530. POMDOCTOR LIMITED Announces Receipt of Nasdaq Notifications Regarding Continued Listing Requirements

GUANGZHOU, China, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- POMDOCTOR LIMITED ("Pomdoctor" or the "Company") (Nasdaq: POM), a digital healthcare company focused on advancing AI-enabled healthcare solutions and predictive healthcare capabilities, today announced that on October 28, 2026, it received two letters (the "Letters") from the Listing Qualifications Department (the "Staff") of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") regarding deficiencies with respect to certain continued listing requirements of The Nasdaq Global Market.

The first Letter notified the Company that, based upon the Company's MVLS for the 30 consecutive business days from September 16, 2026 through October 27, 2026, the Company no longer meets the requirement under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5450(b)(2)(A) to maintain market value of listed securities ("MVLS") of at least $50 million (the "MVLS Requirement"). The Staff also noted that the Company does not meet the requirements under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5450(b)(3) (A).

Pursuant to Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(C), the Company has a compliance period of 180 calendar days, or until April 26, 2027, to regain compliance with the MVLS Requirement. If at any time during the compliance period the Company's MVLS closes at $50 million or more for a minimum of ten consecutive business days, Nasdaq will provide the Company with written confirmation of compliance and the matter will be closed.

The second Letter notified the Company that, based upon the Company's MVPHS for the 30 consecutive business days from September 16, 2026 through October 27, 2026, the Company no longer meets the requirement under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5450(b)(2&3)(C) to maintain a minimum market value of publicly held shares ("MVPHS") of $15 million (the "MVPHS Requirement").

Pursuant to Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(D), the Company has a compliance period of 180 calendar days, or until April 26, 2027, to regain compliance with the MVPHS Requirement. If at any time during the compliance period the Company's MVPHS closes at $15 million or more for a minimum of ten consecutive business days, Nasdaq will provide the Company with written confirmation of compliance and the matter will be closed.

If the Company does not regain compliance prior to the expiration of the applicable compliance period, the Company will receive written notification that its securities are subject to delisting. At that time, the Company may appeal the delisting determination to a Hearings Panel.

The Company intends to monitor its MVLS and MVPHS and evaluate available options to regain compliance with the applicable continued listing requirements within the compliance period.

There can be no assurance that the Company will regain compliance with the applicable Nasdaq continued listing requirements within the compliance period or otherwise maintain compliance with Nasdaq's other continued listing requirements.

POMDOCTOR LIMITED (Nasdaq: POM) is a digital healthcare company focused on advancing AI-enabled healthcare solutions and expanding predictive healthcare capabilities. The Company leverages physician resources, wearable technologies, artificial intelligence, healthcare payment networks and real-world healthcare data to support more personalized, continuous and data-driven healthcare services.

This press release contains forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements include, without limitation, statements concerning the Company's ability and plans to regain and maintain compliance with Nasdaq's continued listing requirements, including the MVLS Requirement and the MVPHS Requirement, the Company's evaluation of alternatives available to regain compliance, and the continued listing of the Company's Class A ordinary shares on Nasdaq.

Forward-looking statements involve risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by such statements. Factors that could cause actual results to differ materially include, among others, the Company's ability to regain and maintain compliance with the MVLS Requirement, the MVPHS Requirement and other Nasdaq continued listing requirements, fluctuations in the market price of the Company's Class A ordinary shares, and the other risks and uncertainties described in the Company's filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Company undertakes no obligation to update any forward-looking statement to reflect events or circumstances occurring after the date of this press release, except as required by applicable law.

#5529. 6 insights from the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative: AI semiconductor industry trends turn the chip race into a systems race

For decades, the semiconductor industry competed on one thing: the individual chip. One of the biggest AI semiconductor industry trends now under way is the shift toward treating chips as components of much larger systems. Performance, cost and reliability are now determined across the package, the rack and the supply chain, not inside a single die.

That shift moves the hardest problems upstream. Packaging, connectivity, yield, sourcing and verification used to come after design, but now they shape it from the first day. AI is shortening development cycles at the same time as it adds to the complexity engineers have to manage. The next phase will be defined by how well companies coordinate across that whole system.

“I think the AI system is our new chips,” said Letizia Giuliano, vice president of product management and marketing at Qualcomm Technologies Inc. “If we were optimizing everything for the silicon in the past, now these days we’re optimizing everything for the system.”

Giuliano and other industry experts spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and co-host Alison Kosik at the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative event in Palo Alto, California. The interviews covered AI semiconductor industry trends, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, AI-driven yield learning, physical AI, strategic sourcing and AI-assisted chip design.

Here are six standout insights from the event:

Moving data between chips, memory and racks now limits AI performance more than raw compute, according to Giuliano. At 200 gigabits per second per lane, half of the signal budget goes just to getting out of the package. That is pushing optical interconnect from rack-to-rack links into the rack, the blade and the package itself, with copper and optics in use side by side. Qualcomm has just launched High Bandwidth Compute, a low-power way to attach compute to memory that is tuned for tokens per watt. Building such products at hyperscale volume means product engineering has to join design-for-test, manufacturing and reliability planning early, explained Sophie Wang, senior director of product engineering at Marvell Technology Inc.

The boundary of an AI system is shifting from the chip to the package, emphasized Nisha Ananthakrishnan, senior director of advanced packaging at Intel Corp. Intel uses its EMIB bridge technology to link chiplets and to scale packages from 3x to more than 10x form factors. Outsourced assembly and test providers are becoming system integrators, noted Patricia MacLeod, senior director of corporate communications and industry partnerships at Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. She pointed to ASE’s VIPack platform, which supports technologies ranging from fan-out chip-on-substrate to co-packaged optics. Many of the chips AI depends on, such as power management chips and voltage regulators built at 12 to 28 nanometers, use mature nodes, added Tazrien Kamal, senior director of technology and innovation at GlobalFoundries Inc.

About 70% to 80% of the problems found when scaling up volume manufacturing could have been caught before tapeout, highlighted Preeti Prasher, chief operating officer of Stathera Inc. Using AI to analyze characterization, simulation and inline manufacturing data lets teams start new wafers before a bad lot reaches test. Adaptive testing also cuts test time. Lattice Semiconductor Corp. has released Lattice Prompt, its first AI design assistant, which turns a plain-language request into a field-programmable gate array design and recommends the best part for the form factor and cost, according to Iliana Chen, senior director of program management at Lattice. Demand from robotics and other markets has made volume Lattice’s biggest challenge, Chen noted.

Physical AI is much broader than humanoid robots and covers any autonomous system that senses its surroundings, reasons and acts in the physical world, explained Gina Longoria, VP of external communications at Arm Ltd. The market is in its first inning, and no single company can build the architecture, security and safety standards it needs on its own, she stressed. Firmware is becoming the layer that ties GPUs, CPUs, network cards and Compute Express Link devices into one fleet-scale system, shared Lakshmi Ramagiri, partner for firmware engineering at Microsoft Corp. Security has to move beyond secure boot to continuous trust while a system is running, and the Open Compute Project and DMTF are the standards bodies to watch, Ramagiri added.

Don’t miss the full interview on theCUBE.

Sourcing now goes well beyond negotiating prices and shapes product development, risk and customer experience, emphasized Alisa Wang, AVP of global planning and procurement at Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd. Because AI-driven demand can change within a year, suppliers have to be treated as strategic partners that receive product roadmaps early, she noted. Leading-edge logic capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. is the tightest constraint, followed by packaging, specialty materials and critical equipment. In response, Credo is qualifying second-source suppliers and spreading its manufacturing footprint across more regions. Stathera’s Prasher highlighted dual sourcing for key segments and using supplier feedback during new product introduction to develop lower-cost products together.

AI is moving from a productivity assistant to a built-in part of electronic design automation flows, explained Rimi Dasgupta, chief of staff for product management and markets at Synopsys Inc., and Vidya Neerkundar, director of product management at Siemens Digital Industries Software. Synopsys has seen verification closure on register-transfer-level designs accelerate as much as 50-fold and debug time drop by 40%, according to Dasgupta. Demand for workload-optimized custom silicon has also cut development cycles from 18 months to six to nine months. AI is probabilistic, but chips must be deterministic, so Synopsys pairs AI with multiphysics solvers from its Ansys acquisition and is working with OpenAI Group PBC on a dedicated GPT-Synopsys model. Multi-die design is the next big shift as chips hit reticle limits, Neerkundar noted.

#5527. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5526. Cooper Standard Adopts Tax Benefits Preservation Plan to Protect its Tax Benefits and Shareholder Value

NORTHVILLE, Mich., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cooper-Standard Holdings Inc. ("Cooper Standard" or the "Company") (NYSE: CPS) today announced that its Board of Directors (the "Board") adopted a tax benefits preservation plan (the "Rights Agreement") in an effort to protect stockholder value by attempting to protect against a possible limitation on the Company's ability to use its net operating loss carryforwards, any loss or deduction attributable to a "net unrealized built-in loss" and other tax attributes (collectively, "Tax Benefits") under the Internal Revenue Code (the "Code").

As of September 30, 2026, Cooper Standard's estimated U.S. Tax Benefits are approximately $215 million, which may be available to offset its future taxable income. The Company views its Tax Benefits as highly valuable assets, which are likely to inure to the benefit of the Company and its stockholders. However, if the Company experiences an "ownership change," as defined in Section 382 of the Code, its ability to use the Tax Benefits could be substantially limited, and the timing of the usage of the Tax Benefits could be substantially delayed, which could significantly impair the value of the Tax Benefits. Generally, an "ownership change" occurs if the percentage of the Company's stock owned by one or more "five percent stockholders" increases by more than fifty percentage points over the lowest percentage of stock owned by such stockholders at any time during the prior three-year period or, if sooner, since the last "ownership change" experienced by the Company.

The Rights Agreement is intended to act as a deterrent to any person acquiring 4.9% or more of the outstanding shares (an "acquiring person") of the Company's common stock without the approval of the Board. This would protect the Tax Benefits because changes in ownership by a person owning less than 4.9% of the common stock are not included in the calculation of "ownership change" for purposes of Section 382 of the Code.

The record date for the distribution of the rights is November 12, 2026. Under the Rights Agreement, the rights will initially trade with the Company's common stock and will generally become exercisable only if a person (or any persons acting as a group) acquires 4.9% or more of the Company's outstanding common stock. If the rights become exercisable, all holders of rights (other than any triggering person) will be entitled to acquire shares of common stock at a 50% discount. Under the Rights Agreement, any person who currently owns 4.9% or more of the Company's common stock may continue to own its shares of common stock but may not acquire any additional shares without triggering the Rights Agreement. Under the Rights Agreement, the Board has the discretion to exempt any transaction and to exempt any person (or group of persons) from the provisions of the Rights Agreement.

The rights expire, unless earlier terminated, on the earliest to occur of: (i) the close of business on November 1, 2029; (ii) the time at which the Rights are redeemed; (iii) the time at which all exercisable Rights are exchanged; (iv) the close of business on November 1, 2027, if the approval of the Company's stockholders of the Rights Agreement has not been obtained by that date; (v) the repeal of Section 382 of the Code if the Board determines that the Rights Agreement is no longer necessary or desirable for the preservation of the Tax Benefits; or (vii) the time at which the Board determines that the Tax Benefits are fully utilized or no longer available under Section 382 of the Code or that an ownership change under Section 382 of the Code would not adversely impact in any material respect the time period in which the Company could use the Tax Benefits, or materially impair the amount of the Tax Benefits that could be used by the Company in any particular time period, for applicable tax purposes.

Additional information about the Rights Agreement is available on a Form 8-K filed by Cooper Standard with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

#5525. Hackers steal $6.3B from Binance in biggest-ever crypto heist

Hackers have stolen about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance, a major cryptocurrency exchange operator.

The heist is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto theft. TRM Labs Inc., a venture-backed blockchain intelligence startup, believes that both cyberattacks were carried out by a North Korean state-backed hacking group tracked as TraderTraitor.

About 40% of the stolen sum comprised stablecoins issued by three major crypto companies: Circle Internet Group Inc., Ripple Labs Inc. and Tether Ltd. They managed to freeze most of the funds before the hackers moved them out of reach. Binance, for its part, has set aside over $6.34 billion to cover users’ losses.

The hackers stole the funds by compromising several of the company’s wallets. One of them powers the infrastructure that Binance uses to process customers’ Ethereum transactions. According to TRM, the hackers breached the wallet late Thursday and sent its entire balance to a wallet they controlled.

TraderTraitor compromised Binance’s wallet by exploiting an Ethereum feature called EIP-7702 that the blockchain’s maintainers released last year. It enables a snippet of code called a smart contract to temporarily control a wallet. EIP-7702 only activates smart contracts if they receive authorization to run from the wallet’s operator. That authorization takes the form of an encrypted message.

The hackers used a malicious smart contract to take over Binance’s Ethereum wallet. It’s currently unclear how they obtained the authorization necessary to run such code.

According to Binance, an internal investigation determined that TraderTraitor had compromised a laptop belonging to one of its DevOps engineers. The company says that it has also “uncovered additional points of breach.”

“Developer and DevOps machines sit close to organizations’ most sensitive systems and hold credentials, tokens and deployment access,” said Kobi Sivilya, chief information security officer of cybersecurity company Checkmarx Ltd. “The question for any organization is how far an attacker could get from a single compromised workstation. Teams should review who has standing access to what systems, whether that access is appropriately limited and whether one machine can reach critical services without a second control.”

TRM determined that TraderTraitor had rehearsed the cyberattack for at least 36 hours before the theft. On Wednesday morning, the hackers deposited a small amount of funds into a malicious crypto wallet. Early Thursday, they tested some of the code that they used in the cyberattack on three different wallets.

According to Binance, the malware contained a “self-destruct mechanism” that deleted the tools the hackers installed on its infrastructure and the activity logs they generated. The mechanism made it more difficult for the company to investigate the attack. Binance did, however, determine that the hackers bypassed the approval workflows it uses to process crypto outflows.

“Organizations that rely on exchanges, custodians or any critical financial counterparty should ask what continuous visibility they have into those relationships,” Rand Davis, chief technology officer at SecurityScorecard, told SiliconANGLE in an email. “They should also ask what their playbook is when a counterparty pauses withdrawals or services. Security leaders can use this moment to map which third parties sit on their critical paths, pressure-test contingency plans, and watch for the phishing and social-engineering follow-on that typically trails a headline event of this scale.”

Binance suspended crypto deposits and withdraws on its exchange after it discovered the breach. The company has since restored deposits, but its withdrawal processing system remains offline. Binance plans to reactivate the feature on Monday.

#5522. Google X co-founder Sebastian Thrun raises $130M for AI engineering startup Dulo

Dulo Inc., a startup co-founded by prominent artificial intelligence researcher Sebastian Thrun, has raised $130 million in funding.

The Information broke the news of the investment on Thursday. Dulo co-founder Adrian Aoun confirmed the report in a post on X.

Before launching Dulo with Thrun (pictured) earlier this year, Aoun sold an early natural language processing startup called Wavii Inc. to Google LLC for over $30 million. He has also invested in companies such as Pinterest Inc. Thrun, in turn, co-founded Google’s X research lab. He led the X program that later became Waymo and helped establish Google Brain, a precursor to Google DeepMind.

Dulo’s round included contributions from former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt and Ram Shriram, one of the search giant’s first investors. They were joined by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, famed venture capitalist John Doerr and more than a half-dozen startup funds. Dulo didn’t disclose its valuation.

The company’s one-page website states that it’s developing foundation models optimized for hardware design tasks. In August, Thrun listed robotics among Dulo’s focus areas. It’s possible the company’s AI is meant to speed up the development of industrial robots and autonomous vehicles.

Thrun joined Google in 2007 after leading the development of Stanley, an early self-driving vehicle that helped kickstart the autonomous driving market. He later founded a flying taxi startup with financial backing from Google co-founder Larry Page.

It’s unclear what hardware design tasks Dulo’s models will automate. One possibility is that the startup hopes to optimize engineering simulations, which hardware teams use to check their product designs for flaws before manufacturing them. Dulo’s website says it’s looking to facilitate “manufacturing at lightspeed.”

Several other engineering-focused AI startups are also working to optimize simulations. One recently funded player, Vinci4D Inc., has built a platform that automates the so-called meshing phase of simulation projects. Meshing is a process through which engineers turn a product’s blueprint into a collection of small, three-dimensional shapes. That arrangement reduces the amount of hardware needed to run simulations.

Other AI startups are working to speed up partially differentiated equations. Simulators rely on such equations to predict the behavior of hardware systems under real-world conditions.

Dulo’s most prominent venture-backed rival is Prometheus Inc., an engineering AI startup co-led by Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos. The company raised $12 billion in funding earlier this year from Bezos and a group of financial institutions. Like Dulo, Prometheus is using AI to speed up the development of complex hardware systems such as robots.

#5519. Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard

Google LLC, Microsoft Corp., Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to support an upcoming website crawling standard.

The technology will enable website operators to block artificial intelligence developers from using their content to train their models.

Many websites contain a text file titled “robots.txt” that informs crawlers what content they may access. A publisher can use the file to block scraping across the board or only make specific webpages inaccessible. It’s also possible to include certain other instructions. For example, a company can ask crawlers not to visit its website too often.

Website operators historically used robots.txt files to manage how search engines interact with their properties. Nowadays, the technology also helps regulate the activity of the scrapers with which AI providers collect training data.

A company that wishes to disallow training-related scraping must make multiple edits to its website’s robots.txt file. In particular, it needs to add a separate entry for every single AI provider. If an AI provider uses multiple scrapers to collect data, each scraper requires its own robots.txt entry.

The crawling standard Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI are backing aims to simplify the process. It would allow website operators to block all scrapers that collect training data for generative AI models with a single robots.txt entry. The setting wouldn’t apply to models that “perform exclusively non-generative tasks.”

The structure of robots.txt files follows a standardized format called the Robots Exclusion Protocol. Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI plan to incorporate  their crawling standard into the format. They have already submitted a draft version of their proposal to the Internet Engineering Task Force, the nonprofit that maintains the Robots Exclusion Protocol.

Microsoft stated in a blog post that it will also provide a crawling setting called AI Grounding. It’s designed for situations where an AI model seeks to access a webpage in order to answer a user question rather than to collect training data.

Microsoft’s setting will enable website operators to prevent its services from sending such requests. The feature will also extend to third-party AI tools that use Microsoft technologies to process prompts.

OpenAI plans to offer similar controls. Both the ChatGPT developer and Microsoft intend to add support for the crawling standard in the coming months, while Google will follow suit sometime next year. Meta Platforms Inc. expressed support for the idea behind the technology but hasn’t yet committed to implementing it.

#5518. Northern California MLSListings joins Compass antitrust fight

MLSListings joined 6 MLSs in an amended SDNY complaint seeking declaratory relief and an injunction to keep enforcing cooperation rules. The suit cites Compass demand letters and threats of litigation over office exclusive marketing.  AI Summary

Yet another MLS is suing Compass International Holdings.

The amended complaint reiterates the claims made in the initial complaint, which was filed by Arizona Regional MLS, Bridge MLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, Hive MLS, and Doorify MLS.

Through this lawsuit, the MLS plaintiffs are asking the court to allow them to continue enforcing their cooperation rules and policies without violating antitrust law, as well as an injunction permanently barring Compass from “bringing or pursuing any claim against any MLS Party alleging that the Cooperation Rules violate the federal antitrust laws or the state antitrust laws.”

As in the initial complaint, the MLSs claim they were prompted to file this lawsuit after Compass sent demand letters to MLSs across the country in early September, threatening to sue them if they did not stop fining or penalizing Compass’s agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin reiterated these threats on stage at the Council of MLSs’ Open House conference in late September, claiming that his firm would spend millions of dollars pursuing litigation against MLSs that refused to comply.

While Compass has contended in public statements and in its recently filed lawsuit against CRMLS, that the MLS is anticompetitive as it is made up of a board of competitors that are creating rules governing how Compass and other members can run their businesses, the six MLS plaintiffs argue that their cooperation rules promote competition among broker members.

In addition, the MLSs contend that the rules help prevent brokers from using the MLS to find buyers while withholding their own listings from free-riding on the contributions of other participants. The complaint also cites the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice‘s 2007 report on competition in real estate brokerage to support its position that MLSs create efficiencies and provide meaningful benefits to consumers.

In an emailed statement, a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that “it’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true.”

“For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?” the spokesperson added. “An agent’s fiduciary duty is to their client, not to the MLS. Only the law and the homeowner should tell real estate professionals how to publicly market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner.”

The claims in this lawsuit are nearly identical to those made in a lawsuit filed earlier in October by California Regional MLS (CRMLS) also in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. Last week, the New York-based OneKey MLS joined CRMLSs lawsuit against Compass.

For its part, Compass has filed its own lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging that the MLS’s rules unlawfully restrict how homeowners and their agents can publicly market properties outside the MLS. The firm has yet to file a lawsuit against another MLS, despite its lingering threats.

Founder of the no-code platform QuintaDB will lead engineering as TrueLoyal changes how it builds and delivers software with AI

SAN ANTONIO, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- TrueLoyalÂ®, the loyalty and advocacy platform for consumer brands, today announced the appointment of Igor Petrushenko as VP of Engineering. Petrushenko will lead TrueLoyal's engineering organization from KrakÃ³w, Poland, as the company puts AI to work across engineering so its team can build and deliver faster for the brands it serves.

Petrushenko founded QuintaDB in 2007 and ran it for 19 years, growing the bootstrapped no-code online database platform from zero into a product serving customers across the EU in 17 languages. He owned it end to end, from the product and architecture to the code, servers, support, and financials. Over the last two years he rebuilt it around AI, including a production multi-agent system that runs the business day to day, features that generate complete apps and websites from a plain-text description, and tools that let AI assistants work with the platform directly. Through all nineteen years, his work has been translating between what a business wants and what a system can do, for customers who did not come to work to configure software.
